05c022e29413.text: By — Rebecca Boone, Associated Press Rebecca Boone, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/many-states-have-backup-execution-plans-but-failures-still-happen Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Many states have backup execution plans, but failures still happen Nation Oct 2, 2026 2:36 PM EDT Long before Christa Pike was brought into Tennessee's execution chamber, prison leaders reviewed and approved a backup plan detailing exactly what to do if the first attempt at lethal injection failed. READ MORE: Christa Gail Pike wasn't Tennessee's first failed execution this year. Here's what to know But the backup plan also failed, and Thursday — 24 hours later — Pike was still alive but in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital, though her prognosis remained uncertain. It's not yet clear what went wrong. Twenty-seven states have capital punishment, and they vary widely in how they administer the death penalty and just how much of that lethal process they keep hidden from public view, according to the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, a clearinghouse for information on U.S. executions. Some states have extensive backup plans. Others don't Tennessee falls somewhere in the middle of the pack when it comes to contingency plans, with two redundancies built into its execution process. First, inmates are supposed to have two intravenous lines placed. Thus, if the first IV site fails, the execution team can switch to the second one. A physician on the execution team can even insert a central line — which typically involves making an incision in a major blood vessel in the groin, neck or armpit in order to thread a catheter into the body to a spot near the heart — if needed. Intravenous lines can fail for several reasons, like a needle and catheter not being properly placed in a vein or wiggling out of place — or a vein rupturing and letting blood and IV fluid leak into tissue surrounding the IV site. Tennessee also allows for a second 100 mg dose of pentobarbital to be administered if the condemned person is still alive five minutes after the first dose was given. Tennessee prison officials gave Pike a second dose, but it's not clear if they used the primary IV site or the backup site to do so. Little backup in Alabama, a lot in Idaho Alabama has a three-drug lethal injection protocol. It allows for a backup dose of the first drug, the sedative midazolam, to be given if the inmate isn't unconscious from the first dose. But the protocol doesn't include additional instructions for what to do if the condemned person is still alive after the first dose of the next two drugs, rocuronium bromide and potassium chloride. WATCH: What we know about Tennessee's botched execution of Christa Pike Idaho, meanwhile, has contingency plans for nearly every step of the execution process, with backup IV sites, allowances for administering a central IV line, and up to three full doses of any of the state's four approved lethal injection drug cocktails. Idaho recently made firing squad its primary execution method, though it has yet to kill someone by that method. Still, the state's firing squad protocol also has a backup plan, with the prison director able to order a second volley of shots within a two-minute time span if she determines it is necessary to complete the execution. Despite contingency plans, executions are still botched at times Idaho called off the execution of Thomas Eugene Creech in 2024 after execution team members could not place a viable IV after eight attempts. Tennessee also called off an execution earlier this year after failing to find a suitable vein for a secondary IV line. In 2014, Arizona executioners injected Joseph Rudolph Wood with a lethal combination of drugs 15 times during the nearly two hours it took him to die. He gasped more than 600 times while he lay on the table. Witnesses keep the public informed when executions succeed or fail In many ways, executions are shrouded in secrecy. The identity of execution team members, the details about where and how lethal drugs are procured, and in some states even what happens in the death chamber is hidden from public view. READ MORE: Tennessee, Oklahoma, Alabama put men to death as U.S. states schedule 3 executions on same day But executions, like all criminal sentences, are conducted by the state on behalf of its citizens, so it's critical that members of the public understand exactly how that ultimate punishment is carried out. Most death penalty states allow a few members of the media to witness executions on behalf of the public. Once the execution is over, those news representatives typically take part in a news conference, sharing exactly what they saw and heard with the rest of the world. Access to executions varies by state, and limitations often lead to court battles Only two states, Indiana and Wyoming, explicitly ban members of the press from witnessing executions. Wyoming, with no one currently on death row, hasn't carried out an execution since 1992, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. A coalition of news organizations including The Associated Press sued Indiana last year for a seat in the witness room, but in June a federal appellate court upheld the state's law barring media access. In Idaho, media witnesses are allowed to watch as a condemned person is placed on a gurney, has IVs inserted and is put to death. Yet AP and other news organizations have sued for increased access. The news organizations asked a judge to allow them to watch via closed-circuit monitors as the drugs are pushed into the IV lines, which is currently shielded from public view in a private room beside the death chamber. A federal judge ordered the state to provide that access, citing a 9th U.S. Circuit Court ruling that said the public should be able to view all critical parts of an execution via the press. But the state appealed, and the appellate court has

8e19a2bc1785.text: Source: Ballotpedia, Congressional Record; Chart: Stef Kight/Axios The Senate is well on its way to claiming the congressional attendance trophy this year, spending 32 more weekdays in session so far than the House. Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) have been torched by members for all the time off — not to mention Democrats, who taunt them for their truancy. The Senate left town late Wednesday — two weeks after its House counterparts — putting both chambers out of town until after the Nov. 3 midterms. "I suppose I left the House two years too soon," Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) told Axios, joking about how many fewer days the House has worked compared to the Senate this Congress. By the numbers: The Senate has been in session for 104 weekdays so far this year, compared with just 72 for the House, according to an analysis of congressional calendars by Ballotpedia and Axios. The Senate has spent nearly 664 hours in session, compared with about 378 hours for the House as of Sept. 14, according to data in the Congressional Record . The House isn't catching up anytime soon: Under the chambers' current calendars, the Senate is on pace to finish the year with about 126 weekdays in session, compared with 92 for the House. Zoom in: Some of the House's time off was unplanned. Johnson has repeatedly sent members home early when his razor-thin majority has run into trouble on the floor, or GOP rebels have blocked passage of a procedural "rule ." Decisions to cut D.C. workweeks short have been met with some backlash. "Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable," Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) wrote on X after Johnson canceled a session day. "The founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid." The other side: Johnson repeatedly argues that his chamber has already done its job. "This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789," Johnson told reporters this month, saying the House had passed more than 900 pieces of legislation and roughly 700 were awaiting Senate action. Johnson's 900-plus figure includes resolutions that can't become law. The Washington Post found the House had passed 732 bills capable of becoming law through Aug. 31. By the numbers: The House passed more measures than the Senate (380 to 269), but the Senate held more "yea" or "nay" votes (231 to 216) between Jan. 3 and the end of August. House members introduced more legislation overall, but the Senate was more productive per capita — 22 pieces of legislation per senator compared to nine per House member. The House has passed 21 bills sent over by the Senate, and the Senate has passed 20 bills sent by the House. The Senate spends significant floor time confirming nominees — which is outside of the House's portfolio.

b99dba56adcd.text: Democrats' dream election scenario risks becoming a nightmare as their candidates in Republican-leaning districts strain to assert their independence from party leadership. Why it matters: Add them to the sizable cohort of outspoken leftists promising to be a thorn in the side of House Democratic leaders, and you get all the ingredients for an unruly majority. "When I see things that I don't think are right, whether they're within my own party or within another party, I'm going to call it out," Jake Johnson, a Democratic House candidate in Minnesota, told Axios in an interview. Montana Democrat Sam Forstag, when asked about the approach he would take on Capitol Hill, said showing a willingness to work across the aisle and "buck your own party" have "got to be a part of it." "There is a tremendous amount of frustration with the D.C. political establishment, and ... a lot of cynicism that things aren't going to change," said Colorado candidate Eileen Laubacher. State of play: Democrats got an early taste last month when Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) repeatedly broke with party leadership on key procedural votes. The defections from a pair of independent-minded frontliners unlocked a new fear for House Democrats: That safe-seat progressives aren't the only rebellious freshmen they will have to worry about next year. It's a salient concern as Democrats put more Republican-leaning seats on their radar in anticipation of a "blue wave" on Election Day. There has been a huge spike in ads from Democrats in those districts repudiating their own party or the two-party system as a whole, Axios reported last week . What they're saying: "I will stand up to Republicans, I will also stand up to Democrats. I talk a lot about this," said Michigan swing-district candidate Christina Hines. Johnson said it's "no wonder people have historically low levels of confidence in Congress" because they "see a bunch of people put on red shirts and blue shirts ... and it's just not working." Forstag pointed to housing as an issue where he has broken with Democrats in his state, telling Axios: "When it comes to zoning reform, you know who I've seen be the biggest impediment to progress? Oftentimes, Democrats." "You bet your ass I'm going to work with Republicans," he said. Between the lines: This swing-district independent streak is bound to come in conflict with the rebellions that safe-seat insurgents are planning. Left-leaning Democratic lawmakers and candidates have told Axios they want votes on core policy issues such as Medicare for All, abolishing ICE and cutting off aid to Israel. The kind of candidate that gets elected to a seat President Trump carried by double digits in 2024 is not going to want to take those votes — in fact, they may be more likely to fund ICE and Israel. Yes, but: Some of these red-seat candidates are quite openly progressive and partisan. The common denominator: They're hearing voters' frustration about party leadership and, if elected, they would arrive on Capitol Hill with a mandate to shake up the system and remain independent. Missouri candidate Fred Wellman, who told Axios he is "very Democrat" and "fairly progressive," said he was "disappointed" that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) met with Jared Kushner in August. Wellman said he will "make a decision when I get there" about whether to vote for Jeffries as speaker and doesn't "intend to be a rubber stamp." Zoom in: Democratic operatives told Axios that this leadership-skeptic attitude extends, in some cases, to candidates not wanting party leaders to come campaign for them. "There's very little appetite for anyone in Democratic leadership," said one consultant of the battleground-district House campaigns they are working with. Matt Herdman, an adviser to Maine Democrat Matt Dunlap, offered Axios a curt response when asked if they would welcome Jeffries to their district: "They haven't offered and we haven't asked." The bottom line: None of this rebelliousness has thus far turned off the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which Jeffries and his leadership allies control. The House Democratic campaign arm has been spending heavily to support Gluesenkamp Perez even after some of her colleagues called for her to be cut off. Fittingly, Gluesenkamp Perez declared in a coordinated ad with the DCCC released Tuesday: "I don't answer to any political party or any president."

b8b27f44413c.text: By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press By — Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/christa-pike-on-a-ventilator-and-unconscious-after-failed-tennessee-execution-attorneys-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Christa Pike on a ventilator and unconscious after failed Tennessee execution, attorneys say Nation Oct 2, 2026 4:24 PM EDT Christa Pike was placed on a ventilator and remained unconscious in a hospital in the hours after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday. Hospital staff, her lawyers said, were working to save Pike's life and as of late Thursday were trying to clear the two doses of the drug that the state uses to execute prisoners. READ MORE: Christa Gail Pike wasn't Tennessee's first failed execution this year. Here's what to know The stunning failure in Tennessee's execution chamber on Wednesday has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an independent review. The court filing offered the first detailed account of Pike's condition after an ambulance carried her away from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on Wednesday night. Her attorneys said a day earlier that she was in critical condition. Christa Pike's attorneys point to problems with the IV Pike's attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream. "Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike's body," they wrote in the court filing. WATCH: What we know about Tennessee's botched execution of Christa Pike Instead of "remedying this failure," they prepared and administered a second dose of pentobarbital, her lawyers said. State officials have not offered any explanations about what went wrong. Tennessee leaders want a review of execution methods Lee demanded a review of the execution procedures and indefinitely postponed Pike's execution and another that had been scheduled for this year. Republican Tennessee lawmakers said the state should review whether to stop single-drug lethal injections and consider other options to carry out death sentences. The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Pike's defense lawyer Randy Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm. Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber's microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt. Pike's attorneys asked a state court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all evidence from the failed execution. "Preserving this evidence is essential to understanding what happened, ensuring accountability and protecting Christa's legal rights," two of her attorneys said in a statement. READ MORE: Many states have backup execution plans, but failures still happen She was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate in a jealous rage. She later became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Following the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, her attorneys said. "It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime," Pike said in an earlier clemency petition. The mother of the 19-year-old woman Pike killed expressed frustration over the failed execution. "I didn't get justice for my daughter," Maya Martinez said Thursday. Problems found with executions four years ago Four years ago, Tennessee's governor ordered another independent review into capital punishment after abruptly stopping the April 2022 execution of Oscar Smith. Lee then paused all executions after acknowledging the state had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were properly tested. Months later, a report found the state hadn't complied with its own lethal injection process since its revision in 2018, resulting in executions being conducted without proper testing of the drugs. READ MORE: Tennessee governor halts executions after Christa Gail Pike survives lethal injection attempt At the time, the state used a three-drug execution protocol of midazolam, vecuronium bromide and potassium chloride. The state later switched to using just pentobarbital. Pentobarbital has been used to carry out death sentences in multiple states and by the federal government. The review, led by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton, also found that the state's unidentified executioner had no formal healthcare training and learned the role mainly through on-the-job experience. After the release of the report, the Tennessee Department of Correction fired its longtime top attorney and another employee. Associated Press writer John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed. Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator on Thursday night, after authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers say in court filings.
Pike, 50, was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance.
Pike remained critically ill and was being treated at a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.
Lawyers for Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, are seeking to have her sentence commuted after the failed execution attempt.
Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution.
Hospital staff are working to save her life and clear the drug - pentobarbital - from her system, the filing states.
During the execution attempt, prison officials attempted to gain intravenous (IV) access by using at least seven needles on Pike, according to her lawyers.
At one point, Pike herself offered guidance of where they could try.
"One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed," the filing states.
While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.
"At one point Ms. Pike stated 'my arm feels like it's about to burst open" and at another asked "'does this happen like that?'"
Pike's attorneys previously warned that her conditions, including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.
In the latest filings, her lawyers allege that "at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike's body".
They are requesting that all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence is preserved.

A New Jersey county has become the latest local government to sue major oil and gas companies, seeking to recover costs from damage caused by worsening flooding and other climate change impacts.
The filing comes just days before the U.S. Supreme Court takes up Boulder, Colorado’s climate case against Big Oil in a proceeding whose outcome could stop these types of lawsuits in their tracks.
Middlesex County is suing ExxonMobil, BP, Chevron, ConocoPhillips, Phillips 66, Shell, and the American Petroleum Institute, following climate deception lawsuits filed by the state of New Jersey and the city of Hoboken. The county’s lawsuit, filed Wednesday in a New Jersey state court, alleges that the defendants’ “decades of climate deception” have exacerbated climate change impacts that are taking a severe toll on the community and costing hundreds of millions of dollars.
“This lawsuit is a necessary step forward to help protect our communities from further damage from extreme weather events,” Middlesex County Commissioner Director Ronald G. Rios said in a statement. “Our residents are not only bearing the costs of damage from flooding and other natural disasters, but also the rising everyday costs of protecting their homes and families from extreme heat and cold. We are taking action to seek compensation.”
County officials told Inside Climate News that the looming Supreme Court ruling did not deter them from moving forward with the lawsuit. “Middlesex County is positioning itself to advance quickly once the Supreme Court makes its decision on this matter,” Rios said in an emailed statement. “This is the right action to take on behalf of our hardworking residents.”
The American Petroleum Institute called the county’s lawsuit “baseless” and said it is part of a “coordinated campaign against an industry that powers everyday life, drives America’s economy, and is actively reducing emissions.”
“We continue to believe that climate policy belongs in Congress, not a patchwork of courtrooms,” API senior vice president and general counsel Ryan Meyers said in a statement.
The other defendants did not respond to requests for comment.
The county, New Jersey’s second most populous, has experienced at least 60 significant flooding events linked to coastal storms and extreme rainfall in recent decades, wreaking over $500 million in property damage. Three major storms alone—Irene, Sandy and Ida—caused the county government to incur nearly $200 million in damages and related costs.
The lawsuit’s filing comes in the wake of a climate change-fueled nor’easter last weekend that battered parts of the mid-Atlantic and Northeast, including the Jersey Shore. Some New Jersey towns recorded over a half foot of rain; several towns in Middlesex County saw over 4 inches of rainfall. Scientists say rising sea levels from climate change made flooding from the storm even worse.
The county says it is also experiencing more days of extreme heat, and this summer, hazardous smoke from Canadian wildfires that drifted into the Northeast region caused the worst air-quality readings in New Jersey’s history.
“Middlesex County has been reeling from the devastating impact of one climate disaster after another,” the complaint states. “And there is no end in sight. Middlesex County will continue to feel the disastrous effects of the raging climate crisis that Defendants have spent decades trying to conceal.”
The lawsuit brings claims of nuisance, trespass and negligence as well as violations of New Jersey’s Consumer Fraud Act.
More than two dozen similar cases have been filed against major fossil fuel entities over the past nine years by cities, counties, states, Native American tribes and individuals. The lawsuits cite evidence revealed through investigations by Inside Climate News and others showing that companies like Exxon knew decades ago that unchecked fossil fuel use could cause “catastrophic” climate harm, yet concealed these risks from the public to inflate sales and protect their profits.
On Monday, the Supreme Court will hear arguments in the Suncor v. Boulder case, which involves state tort claims brought by the city and county of Boulder against oil companies Suncor and ExxonMobil over localized climate impacts. The companies argue that federal law preempts these claims, and if a majority of the justices agree, the ruling could knock out not only Boulder’s case but others like it, including Middlesex County’s.
“The outcome of this decision will have enormous consequences for communities already saddled with funding the massive costs of adapting to a changing climate,” Pat Parenteau, emeritus professor of law at Vermont Law and Graduate School, wrote in a new piece published in The Conversation.
“A broad ruling in favor of Suncor could effectively kill dozens of similar climate-deception lawsuits filed by cities, counties and states nationwide,” Parenteau added. “That would leave the public on the hook for billions of dollars to cope with the escalating impacts of climate change.”

During this past summer of climate extremes, more than half of Europe experienced dangerous levels of heat stress, the combined effect of temperature, humidity, wind and sunshine on the body’s ability to cool itself. In some places, that amounted to a “feels like” temperature of 100 degrees Fahrenheit or higher.
The heat stress spread across a record extent of 52 percent of the continent, the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service announced in a Friday news bulletin. The May-to-August period also brought record-low flows in many major European rivers and widespread losses of important food crops, including grain.
The higher the heat stress index, the harder it becomes for the human body to regulate its temperature, said Peter Hoffmann, a senior scientist and meteorologist with the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. The measurement captures the magnitude and spatial extent of heatwave impacts in detail, he said.
But temperatures remain a key factor, he added, and last summer, 37 percent of European land areas experienced all-time daily, monthly or seasonal temperature records, extending across nearly all of England and Wales, and from France and Spain across Italy, Switzerland and Austria.
The summer was so extreme that four of Western Europe’s 10 most severe heatwaves since 1950 occurred between late May and mid-August 2026. All four were more intense than Europe’s landmark 2003 heatwave, although they differed in duration and spatial extent.
Samantha Burgess, a climate expert with the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said the summer brought compounding extremes to Europe, affecting water supplies, energy systems, transport, ecosystems and agriculture, along with human health.
The report also concluded that the heat season is expanding into the spring and fall. In May and September, more than 40 percent of Europe experienced temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 degrees Celsius), a benchmark for heat on a continent historically known for a temperate climate.
Across 12 major river systems, the total discharge volume was about 69 cubic kilometers below the long-term mean, equivalent to roughly two years of public water supplies across the European Union. The Loire, Seine, Rhine, Glomma, Vistula and Danube rivers recorded their lowest summer-average flows on record at their outlets. Long stretches of the Rhône, Po, Dniester, Elbe and Dnieper rivers also experienced record-low flows.
By the end of August, around 46 percent of European land was experiencing drought conditions, and around 40 percent of the affected area was classified as being under extreme drought.
Several rapid climate attribution assessments this summer found that human-caused warming intensified all the extremes, making the heatwaves hotter and more likely than in the past.
An analysis of the June heatwave led by World Weather Attribution scientists found that human-caused warming raised the daytime highs by nearly 4 degrees Fahrenheit. Other climate research suggests that global warming is shifting large-scale wind patterns into directions that spawn more heatwaves over Europe.
“The summer of 2026 shows that we are lagging behind in adapting to climate change in many areas,” said Fred Hattermann, a hydroclimatic risk expert with the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. The adaptation gap is evident in the disruption to transportation from low river flows, and in the wildfires that raged out of control in France, he said.
“It’s not that there’s no investment in adaptation, but it’s often fragmented and not coordinated on a larger regional scale,” he added. “With climate change advancing rapidly, we’re having great difficulty implementing these measures quickly enough.”

A former US congressman has been sentenced to 10 years in a federal prison for money laundering and working as an undeclared foreign agent.
David Rivera, 61, who was elected as a Florida Republican, was found guilty in May after a seven-week trial heard Venezuela's state-run oil company hired his consulting firm to lobby members of Congress to help improve US relations with Venezuela.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a former housemate of Rivera, and Texas congressman Pete Sessions both testified to the court that they had no idea about his activities.
Defence lawyers had said the lobbying was for a US subsidiary of the oil company, not the Venezuelan government.
Rivera's associate, political consultant Esther Nuhfer, who was tried alongside him, was also found guilty in the case.
As a part of his sentence, Rivera, who served in Congress from 2011-13, must also forfeit his Florida properties.
Federal prosecutors in Florida said Rivera and Nuhfer engaged in a "secret political influence campaign", receiving a $50m (Â£37m) contract for three months of work on behalf of a US-based subsidiary of Venezuelan state oil firm PDVSA, which is also known as Citgo.
Prosecutors alleged that, in 2017 and 2018, at the behest of former Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro's government, Rivera and Nuhfer attempted to lobby Rubio - then still a senator and former housemate of Rivera - as well as Kellyanne Conway, a former senior White House adviser.
The lobbying came during a moment of tense relations between the US and Venezuela, during President Donald Trump's first term in the White House when his administration imposed sanctions on the South American country.
Defence lawyers for Rivera and Nuhfer argued that the pair did not need to register as foreign agents because their contract was with a US-based subsidiary of a Venezuelan state company.
But Judge Melissa Damian said during Friday's sentencing: "There's no dispute this money came from the Maduro regime."
Rubio, who was not implicated in the wrongdoing, testified during the trial that he was close friends with Rivera but was unaware he was working as a lobbyist.

Hawaii's famous HÅlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean.
The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said.
"The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement.
Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination.
The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend.
The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 KÄ«lauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch.
Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline".
In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said.
Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland."
Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it.
"Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now."

5e09a0888930.text: Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios Christa Pike 's survival after two lethal injection doses has put state execution protocols nationwide under new scrutiny. The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state , with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized. Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method , accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method. Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee. Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method. Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods. Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders. Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years. Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

The so-called “lame duck” session of Congress after November’s midterm elections could be momentous for clean energy as lawmakers are set to consider a long-sought bipartisan deal to speed permitting of large energy and infrastructure projects.
Clean energy advocates and policy experts view the bill as a rare opportunity to deal with a major clean energy roadblock—long queues for interconnection to the grid. But division emerged immediately among environmental advocates, with some arguing the measure would weaken state and tribal government authority and allow pipelines and other fossil fuel projects to take advantage of a streamlined process.
This tension is not unusual. A version of it happened during debate over what would become the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, also known as the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, and the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022 under President Joe Biden.
“These policy bills have to get 60 Senate votes, so they have to be bipartisan, and so necessarily you’re going to be in a situation [in which there are] things that members like and things they don’t like,” said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies, a consulting firm that specializes in federal energy issues. The 60-vote threshold in the Senate is the number needed to overcome either party’s ability to block legislation with a filibuster.
Gramlich considers the bill a big step forward for renewable energy because of technology-neutral provisions that would “enable many tens of gigawatts of clean energy to be connected that otherwise are unable to develop,” he said.
Also supporting the bill is Pete Wyckoff, vice president of policy for Evergreen Action, an environmental advocacy group. He also played a key role in developing the Inflation Reduction Act when he worked for Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn.
“America can’t confront the climate crisis and meet growing energy demand unless we can build clean energy faster—and that means fixing how we permit it,” Wyckoff said in a statement.
Some of the Senate’s most vocal members on climate change co-wrote the measure.
“If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, said in a statement. “Like all major pieces of bipartisan legislation, this bill is a compromise. We believe it is a compromise that will result in a brighter, cleaner, more affordable future.”
Whitehouse and the bill’s other co-authors are calling it the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.
Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., maintained that the bill would continue to protect land, water and wildlife while transforming the nation’s ability to fuel future growth. “For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth,” Capito said in a statement.
A Post-Election Vote Plan
After months of working to hammer out their permitting compromise, Capito, Whitehouse and their partners on the deal—Senate Energy Committee leaders Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, and Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.—made clear they had run out of time to get the package to a vote before the midterm election.
That kicks the legislation to the final weeks of the 119th Congress, and possibly—depending on the November results—the last session of unified Republican control.
This creates some political peril for the package, clean energy lobbyist Chris Moyer, founder of Echo Communications Advisors, pointed out in a newsletter to his clients. “The question for the lame duck, especially with House Democrats, is whether we experience a repeat of the familiar cycle,” Moyer wrote. “The party on the verge of taking power holds out until the new Congress to get a ‘better’ bill.”
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Moyer noted that Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, expressed exactly this sentiment in a post on X. “We can’t throw states, tribes, impacted communities, and threatened and endangered wildlife under the bus,” said Huffman, who pledged to work for a better bill in the next Congress.
But history has shown lame-duck sessions can forge compromises that wouldn’t be possible in regular sessions of Congress, in part because departing members will not face repercussions from voters. Among the historic environmental measures that passed Congress during lame-duck sessions were the Superfund toxic waste clean-up bill in 1980 and the establishment of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration in 1970.
The Challenge in the Senate
The most significant challenge the legislation faces may be securing enough Democratic votes in the Senate in the face of opposition from some environmentalists. Even before the text of the legislation was released, the Western Environmental Law Center released a statement labeling the deal a “five-alarm fire” that would allow artificial intelligence data centers and energy infrastructure to proliferate. Among the changes the legislation would make is limiting state and tribal officials from using their authority under the Clean Water Act to address issues unrelated to direct water pollution; the Trump administration proposed a similar regulatory change earlier this year.
“The permitting deal is a betrayal of public lands, water and wildlife, and environmental justice values that Westerners depend on for clean air and water, places to hike, hunt, and fish, and the inestimable sense of freedom the West provides us all,” said Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, executive director of the center.

More than 20 states, including North Carolina, New York, California and Pennsylvania, as well as several cities, are suing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over its repeal of most greenhouse gas emissions standards for coal- and natural gas-fired power plants. The agency’s proposal would also thwart future administrations from reinstating the rule.
The state attorneys general, all of them Democrats, filed the lawsuit Oct. 1 in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. The plaintiffs are asking the court to review the proposed rescission.
In a press release, New York Attorney General Letitia James said the coalition is arguing that the administration’s actions are “clearing the way for millions of additional tons of greenhouse gas emissions that will worsen extreme heat, deadly storms, flooding, and wildfires.” The coalition includes Washington, D.C., Chicago, Denver and New York City.
The EPA told Inside Climate News it does not comment on pending litigation.
“We applaud Attorney General Jackson’s leadership in protecting our air quality and safeguarding public health,” said Jeffrey Robbins, executive director of the nonprofit CleanAIRE North Carolina, of North Carolina’s Attorney General Jeff Jackson. “Joining this lawsuit sends a clear message: North Carolina will not stand by while federal rollbacks force our families to pay higher costs at the pump for dirtier air. Our health should not be secondary to fossil fuel industry profits.”
Duke Energy operates five coal-fired power plants in North Carolina and 17 fueled by natural gas.
In announcing the proposed rule, the agency argued that it lacks the legal authority under the Clean Air Act to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, the largest stationary sources of the pollutants.
That’s not true, said John Broderick, an assistant attorney general in the New York Environmental Protection Bureau, during an Oct. 1 EPA public hearing on the proposed rule. The agency not only has the authority, Broderick said, it has a “statutory duty to regulate greenhouse gases from power plants.” He called the EPA’s move “a blatantly unlawful attempt to undermine the Clean Air Act.”
Greenhouse gas emissions drive climate change, which causes or worsens extreme weather, such as heat waves, droughts, floods and storms. This year’s Super El Niño is contributing to heat and strong hurricanes in the Pacific, but its effects are amplified by global warming.
August 2026 was the planet’s hottest August since recordkeeping began in 1850, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Western Europe endured five heat waves this summer, with temperatures at times exceeding 104 degrees Fahrenheit.
Amy Laura Cahn is a special assistant attorney general for the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, focused on energy and the environment.
During the public hearing, Cahn told the EPA the proposal is “wrong on the law, wrong on the science and wrongly ignores the harms it will cause and will be felt first and worst by our most marginalized communities.”
Massachusetts is a primary reason that greenhouse gas emissions regulations exist. In 2007, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a landmark case against the EPA that the agency could legally regulate greenhouse gas emissions if it determines they endanger public health and welfare—which it did two years later.
Now the EPA says the scientific and legal foundation for these rules is flawed, an argument rebutted by major scientific organizations and legal experts.
“Carbon emissions contribute to climate change,” Cahn said. “Flawed and unsupported analysis can’t undermine reality.”
The EPA estimates that the repeal would save the power sector $95 billion to $160 billion in compliance costs over the next 20 years. The savings do not account for benefits such as ensuring electric grid reliability and other benefits that cannot be monetized, the EPA said.
Those estimates exclude the health and environmental costs of greenhouse gas emissions—and the financial benefits of reining in the pollutants. The Biden administration calculated the rules would save $370 billion in climate and public health costs through 2047.
“Erasing these standards doesn’t save money,” said Robbins of CleanAIRE NC in a prepared statement. “It simply transfers the financial burden from corporate polluters onto the backs of patients, families and ratepayers.”
This is the second instance in which the EPA has weakened rules governing greenhouse gas emissions. Earlier this year the agency revoked the endangerment finding for the pollutants related to motor vehicles.
“Federal rollbacks make state leadership more urgent than ever,” Robbins said. “We cannot rely on this administration to protect the air we breathe.”

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. The Scoop
On June 1, OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon gave employees a preview of a blog post denying the company had any connection to Leading the Future, a super PAC established to defend AI from regulation. OpenAI president Greg Brockmanâs support for the super PAC âhas been in a personal capacity, not on behalf of the company,â Kwon wrote in an internal Slack message.
Not everyone on his staff bought it. One OpenAI employee took to Slack to warn of a dangerous trade-off: The companyâs aggressive political activity threatened to drive researchers to Anthropic, and hamstring OpenAI in the all-out race to recursively self-improving AI. The post earned 24 âagreeâ reactions and a solitary eyes emoji.
The next day, Kwon gave ground to a different internal critic: The company, he said on Slack, was âtaking reputational hits.â They had drawn âsome clear public lines,â but âI wish weâd done it even sooner.â
Ten days after Kwonâs post, Brockman backed out of the second half of his public $50 million commitment, saying he felt âterrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the companyâ in a post first reported by The New York Times. Brockmanâs message received 40 hearts, five checkmarks, and three thank-you emojis.
The episode, part of a set of Slack messages shared with Semafor, offers a window into the complex internal politics of the handful of companies shaping the global future of artificial intelligence. Outsiders observing the tribal world of San Francisco frontier labs often see OpenAI as the âaccelerationistâ cousin to the safety-oriented Anthropic.
The rare glimpse inside the companyâs Slack illustrates a more complex reality: Many of OpenAIâs developers, engineers, and researchers âÂ whom the company is fighting to keep in intense talent wars whose bidders also include Meta, Google, and an array of startups âÂ arenât sanguine about unregulated AI. And they dislike being associated with the political groupâs aggressive tactics.
A spokeswoman for OpenAI declined to comment.
One employee initially placated by Kwonâs post followed up two days later flagging that Brockmanâs money would be used to fund an X account the employee described as âan LTF sockpuppet (confirmed here) that posts stuff like â[sam altman is] a caterpillar that murders insects and stitches their dismembered body parts onto its back as armor.â (Twenty-two other employees responded, âWTF.â)
A source familiar with the situation told Semafor that employee pushback was definitely part of Brockmanâs decision, but that he had his own qualms that began with LTF targeting New York Assemblymember Alex Bores, an AI safety advocate running for Congress in New York. The person said that Brockman had expected the PAC to focus more on supporting allied candidates.
The people running LTF appeared not to understand the complex internal dynamics of frontier safety policy âÂ and how the whole industry would react to attacking someone running on that platform. At different points, the person added, Brockman gave pointed feedback to LTF; the source noted they hadnât heard of the PAC attacking candidates since Bores.
Since then, the PAC has overwhelmingly donated to front-runners in congressional races. And candidates LTF has endorsed or implicitly supported have come out in favor of a bill from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar that would pause frontier AI development and criminalize attempting to build superintelligence, OpenAIâs stated goal.
Leading the Future
LTF launched in August 2025, well before AI became a major public issue. The group boasted more than $100 million in commitments, with $50 million to come from Brockman and his wife Anna. OpenAIâs global affairs chief Chris Lehane had helped set up the PAC, which followed a model he pioneered for the crypto industry.
OpenAI sought to characterize the PAC as a totally independent entity, but employees âÂ encouraged by critics on X âÂ were skeptical. Staff were complaining about the connection in February, Wired reported, and Transformer reported that employees confronted Lehane in a meeting in May, pushing the company to explain its relationship with LTF.
Kwonâs June 1 Slack message sought to defuse the controversy.
âMany have posted questions,â he wrote, about the nature of the relationship between OpenAI and LTF. At the end of the multi-paragraph message, he concluded, âThank you to everyone who has given feedback on this topic and pushed for a stronger company statement, in particularâ before tagging three employees.
It worked â for about an hour. More than 80 employees reacted with approving emojis, and the first reply was excited and appreciative. But then others questioned the groupâs independence, highlighted LTFâs controversial and backfiring track record, and worried about the super PACâs toxic effect on OpenAIâs brand and retention of senior researchers.
The messages were shared with Semafor on the condition that they not be quoted directly out of concern that employees would feel uncomfortable seeing their messages reproduced verbatim, potentially chilling future Slacktivism.
The dispute flared up again on June 11. One worker posted a Transformer article in which the director of LTFâs sister lobbying group, Build American AI (BAAI), which does not disclose its donors, texted journalist Veronica Irwin, âFor this project Iâm funded by four separate entities â¦ OpenAI is just one of themâ (OpenAI told Irwin and other journalists that the company had not provided funding to the groups).
Just over an hour later, Brockman weighed in for the first time, denying the storyâs claim that OpenAI backed BAAI and assuring staff that heâd given nothing to the organization (though as employees noted later in the thread, LTF gives money to BAAI). He then apologized for how LTF reflected on the company and abandoned his additional $25 million donation.

60338614e8ab.text: By — Maria Ramirez Uribe Maria Ramirez Uribe Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/supreme-court-ready-to-tackle-climate-immigration-and-gun-rights-here-are-5-cases-to-watch Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Supreme Court ready to tackle climate, immigration and gun rights. Here are 5 cases to watch Politics Oct 2, 2026 5:45 PM EDT When the U.S. Supreme Court returns Monday, the justices will kick off a new term featuring cases on climate change, gun rights, immigration and religious liberty. The high court has agreed so far to hear 30 cases, after a summer that PBS News Supreme Court analyst and SCOTUSblog co-founder Amy Howe called not "much of a 'recess.'" Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Historically, Supreme Court justices have a quiet summer after they've finished publishing the previous term's decisions in June. They then decide which cases they'll hear in the new term. But a rising surge of petitions to the emergency docket, also known as the "shadow docket," mean justices must quickly issue temporary decisions while cases make their way through the lower court system. These decisions are usually unsigned and don't provide extensive explanations. WATCH: New book 'Shadow Docket' explores Supreme Court's growing influence on American law "Compared with past years, they hear relatively few cases on the 'merits,' and a lot of their work takes place on the emergency docket, which, although theoretically 'temporary,' can have long-term effects for the litigants involved," Howe said. In September, for example, the high court temporarily blocked Trump's effort to restrict mail-in voting in an emergency docket ruling. The Supreme Court is likely to add more cases for arguments in the coming months, as it has in the past, such as in April 2025, when the court announced it would hear a case on nationwide injunctions related to the Trump administration's birthright citizenship policy. This term, Howe said, the Supreme Court could still add cases related to the military's ban on transgender members or President Donald Trump's appeal on his defamation case brought by writer E. Jean Carroll. Here's a look at five significant cases going before the Supreme Court this term. Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County: Can corporations be held liable for climate change? The first case to go before the Supreme Court this term deals with whether state and local governments can sue energy companies over their role in climate change. The county and city governments of Boulder, Colorado, sued Suncor and Exxon Mobil in 2018, alleging the companies knew they were contributing to climate change and caused harm to the county, city and its residents. Boulder is seeking monetary compensation from the companies. The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments Oct. 5. Listen in our video player above. There are dozens of similar cases around the country where state and local municipalities are seeking billions of dollars in damages, Howe said. READ MORE: Should big oil pay for climate damage? Some cities and states say yes The Supreme Court will now decide whether Boulder can sue the energy companies under state law. The companies say the suits are barred by federal law and the U.S. Constitution. Lower courts have ruled that the cases belong in state, not federal courts, according to the Congressional Research Service. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from the case on Sept. 28. Viramontes v. Cook County: Can states implement bans on AR-15s? In December, the court will hear arguments over the legality of a local Illinois law banning possession, sale and transfer of assault weapons, including AR-15s. County residents and gun rights organizations sued the locality in 2021, saying the law infringed upon their constitutional rights. The Supreme Court will decide whether the Second and 14th Amendments give people the right to possess semiautomatic weapons. READ MORE: Supreme Court will consider whether AR-15 bans violate the Second Amendment The case's importance transcends whether semiautomatic weapons can be banned, David French, a lawyer and New York Times columnist, said during a SCOTUSblog event. "The vast majority of jurisdictions in the United States, even if you're able to ban an AR-15, don't ban AR-15s," French said. "The democratic process has kind of worked its way through in the gun control arena." This case is about whether the court will further clarify its jurisprudence on the Second Amendment, "which is still in its relative infancy," Howe said. "The Supreme Court has remained largely silent on the scope and meaning of the Second Amendment" for more than 200 years, according to the Congressional Research Service. Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.: Can immigrants be deported to countries where they have no ties? With this case, the Supreme Court will weigh in on the Trump administration's policy to deport immigrants to countries other than their own. The court originally took the case up as part of its emergency docket and issued a ruling on Sept. 29 allowing Trump to continue third-country deportations. READ MORE: Supreme Court lets Trump continue deporting people to 3rd countries while justices consider policy In the coming months it will hear arguments and rule on the legality of the policy and whether immigrants have the right to object before deportation. Trump has sent thousands of immigrants to countries to which they have no ties, where they are denied due process and face human rights abuses, according to advocacy organizations. Rhoney v. The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.
President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.
But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the coordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".
Macron said the coordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".
In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.
The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.
The G7 leaders said they will also coordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped Â£2 a litre for the first time on Friday.
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.
The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.
Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

e5b4a775139f.text: By — Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/judge-halts-border-wall-construction-in-texas-big-bend-region-for-now Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge halts border wall construction in Texas' Big Bend region for now Nation Oct 2, 2026 7:10 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal court in Texas on Friday issued a ruling temporarily blocking the Trump administration from building a border wall and other infrastructure across the state's Big Bend region, in a victory for opponents who have pushed back against what has long been a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump. Landowners, businesses and environmentalists in the region have united to oppose the planned infrastructure projects, which are part of a $46 billion effort by the Trump administration to line the southern border with a mix of 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers, roads and surveillance technology. READ MORE: Trump administration begins building border wall in Big Bend region of Texas The judge's ruling includes Big Bend National Park, which sits on a bend of the Rio Grande River, but also extends across the entire, roughly 500-mile-long Big Bend sector, which accounts for about a quarter of the roughly 2,000-mile-long southern border with Mexico. Judge Kathleen Cardone said in her ruling that the plaintiffs were "likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of the claims in suit, that there is a likelihood that they will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor." Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Opponents of the border wall project have argued that the Big Bend region of Texas is so remote and the landscape so rugged that it serves as its own deterrent to illegal immigration and that the administration violated the law when it issued a swath of waivers allowing it to bypass numerous regulations in order to speed up border wall infrastructure projects. The lawsuit brought by an environmental organization, advocates for a historic church in Ruidosa and a river guide argued that the Department of Homeland Security was wrong to bypass regulations meant to protect the environment, culture, and archeology of regions like the Big Bend area. Laiken Jordahl, with the Center of Biological Diversity that brought the suit, called Cardone's ruling a "total victory." "The bulldozers are going to be sent packing until she rules on the merits," Jordahl said. "This is such a historic day for Big Bend and for Texas and the Constitution." The court's decision comes just weeks after the administration erected the first border wall panels in the Big Bend sector in mid-September. The border wall project through the Big Bend sector has sparked bipartisan opposition. Much of the opposition has been geared around Customs and Border Protection's plans for inside the Big Bend National Park, which is prized for its beautiful landscapes, limestone cliffs and crystal clear night sky views. When bulldozers were spotted clearing land in the park in August, it sparked widespread opposition with both Republicans and Democrats calling for the administration to stop. Customs and Border Protection paused all activity there, but that pause expired on September 30. The administration has said it's reevaluating plans for the National Park but has not yet said what it will do there. Advocates for the park on Friday said they were happy with the judge's ruling but called on the administration to fix the damage already done to Big Bend National Park, come to the table to meet with local residents and develop alternative plans. "Big Bend is no place for border barriers. It's time for the administration to come to the table with the border communities that know Big Bend best, repair the damage from this ill-conceived project, and find new solutions," said Tiernan Sittenfeld, National Parks Conservation Association President and CEO in a statement. The judge's ruling extends to areas up and downriver from the National Park, where Customs and Border Protection has planned a range of border infrastructure projects that would largely require building across privately owned land. In those areas, the government has been working to obtain permission from local landowners to survey and build on their land, but in a recent court filing, it said it was prepared to refer some cases to the Justice Department where it hadn't been able to secure permission from landowners. 483af27c04b4.text: Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces are planning a major counteroffensive against Iran-backed Houthis in the coming days — an effort to push them away from areas on the Red Sea coast that control the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb, two U.S. officials say. Why it matters: For the second time in recent weeks, the U.S. rebuffed Saudi pleas to join the operation and conduct airstrikes. But U.S. officials say that could change if the operation runs into problems. The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. Control over it gives the Houthis and their Iranian backer a powerful new point of leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Driving the news: In recent weeks, the Houthis took over key areas of the southern Red Sea coast that control the strait. They also increased missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia. The Saudis retaliated with airstrikes against Houthi targets. Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the Saudis have been planning the operation for weeks and that plans were approved by Saudi leadership several days ago. The operation will include ground forces loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen with Saudi air cover. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid Bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the U.S. official said. A U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now." Last week, President Trump was close to ordering a strike on the Houthis after a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), but eventually decided to hold off . Between the lines: Trump is caught between wanting to help his friend and ally MBS, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen and saw it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. Zoom in: U.S. officials say the U.S. military is helping the Saudis with everything short of direct combat, mainly intelligence and targeting data. One U.S. official said that in the last two weeks, the U.S. military provided the Saudis with more than 200 Houthi targets to strike. The official said the strikes significantly increased pressure on the Houthis.

EL PASO—Federal Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction Friday to halt construction on the border wall in Texas’ expansive Big Bend sector, including the national and state parks.
Cardone read a brief order from the bench after hearing more than four hours of testimony from conservation groups and residents of the Big Bend region, known internationally for its dark night skies, abundant biodiversity and rugged river canyons.
Cardone said that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits in at least one of their claims and to suffer irreparable harm if construction continues. Her ruling stops border barrier construction in the entire Big Bend sector—which spans more than 500 miles across West Texas—until the federal government complies with all applicable laws.
The ruling applies to all of Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and the border along the Rio Grande in the rest of the sector. The injunction will remain in place while the court considers the lawsuit, which was filed in April.
Plaintiffs and their supporters embraced and wept outside the federal courtroom in El Paso Friday afternoon following the ruling. Many had traveled hundreds of miles from Big Bend communities, including Terlingua and Marfa, to attend.
The Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church and Danny Miller Jr., a river guide, sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and Secretary Markwayne Mullin for waiving dozens of laws to fast-track the border wall through the Big Bend region. The Texas Civil Rights Project and the Center for Biological Diversity are representing the plaintiffs.
The federal waivers cover the entire Big Bend region. This had allowed construction to proceed without following the National Environmental Policy Act, the Archaeological and Historic Preservation Act and many other laws. Under the injunction, the effect of the waivers is stayed.
Customs and Border Protection has changed its plans for border barrier construction in the Big Bend region numerous times since February. The federal government currently plans to build vehicle barriers and access roads within the state and national parks. A 30-foot steel wall is planned for private land in Big Bend outside the parks.
In mid-August, advocates documented excavators and bulldozers clearing land within Big Bend National Park. Customs and Border Protection then issued a construction pause in the park on Aug. 17. That pause lifted this week. Construction recently began on a new 30-foot steel wall in Hudspeth County, east of El Paso.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs called eight people to testify Friday. Their arguments centered on the lack of evidence that the Big Bend sector is an area of “high illegal entry,” as stated in the federal waivers. They argued that the plaintiffs were already suffering and will continue to suffer harm if border wall construction continues.
Adam Isaacson, an analyst at the Washington Office on Latin America, presented data showing the Big Bend sector is a “distant last place” in unauthorized border crossings compared to the nine sectors that make up the U.S. border with Mexico. The plaintiffs’ attorneys explained that they requested granular data about how many people are detained in Big Bend National Park, as opposed to the vast area that makes up the rest of the sector, and the federal government never supplied that information.
Miller, the river guide, said his business depends on access to the Rio Grande and explained how property he owns along the river will be irrevocably damaged if the wall is built.
He described border wall construction as a “visible scar that will never go away.” Miller and several other individuals giving testimony broke down in tears when asked how a border wall could change their relationship to the Rio Grande.
U.S. Department of Justice attorneys presented few counterarguments and did not present any witnesses. The White House referred questions to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said. “We are working with the Department of Justice on next steps.”

"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."
