Only three teams remain unbeaten in the NFL after two more 100% starts were halted during week four of the season.
Sunday's slate got under way with the Indianapolis Colts beating the Washington Commanders in the first of this season's three London games.
The New England Patriots and Los Angeles Rams then avoided dropping to a 1-3 record by pulling off some big wins on the road.
The Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders were among the five teams who made a 3-0 start to the season and one team's '0' had to go as the divisional rivals met, while the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings marched on.
Here are five things you missed from Sunday's action.
Raiders push Chiefs all the way
Kansas City have dominated their rivalry with the Raiders in recent years, but Las Vegas are vastly improved after winning only three games last season and pushed the Chiefs all the way.
The Raiders led 13-10 heading into the final quarter in Vegas, which featured three lead changes before Kansas City held on for a 30-27 win.
The turning point came as new running back Kenneth Walker maintained his stunning start by scoring two touchdowns in 19 seconds, with the Chiefs regaining possession immediately by forcing a fumble on the kick-off return.
The Raiders gave themselves hope with a Brock Bowers score and stayed alive until the final play, when Kirk Cousins was tackled as he threw and his wayward pass was intercepted.
Walker finished with 177 yards from 22 carries, while team-mate Tyquan Thornton also had two touchdowns and 111 receiving yards.
After missing last season's play-offs, the Chiefs look capable of getting back into Super Bowl contention. They next face the Los Angeles Chargers, who are 0-4 after losing 30-23 to defending champions the Seattle Seahawks.
49ers and Vikings march on
The other two teams who improved to 4-0 were the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings.
The 49ers hosted the Denver Broncos, who overcame Super Bowl favourites the Rams last week, and they were tied 3-3 until late in the third quarter.
Christian McCaffrey's touchdown in the fourth quarter gave the 49ers some breathing space and, although Jaylen Waddle replied, George Kittle scored on a huge catch-and-run down the middle to seal a 24-14 win.
While Cousins and Brock Purdy lead the league with 11 touchdown passes, Purdy has been intercepted only once and has not been sacked in the 49ers' first four games.
The Vikings are the biggest surprise to be 4-0, having ground out another win, this time 15-10 over the Miami Dolphins, with Will Reichard kicking five field goals.
Maye bounces back
Some said Drake Maye's confidence was shot after he was benched during the New England Patriots' blowout loss at the Jacksonville Jaguars last week.
After throwing eight interceptions in the 2025 regular season, the 24-year-old quarterback had six in the Patriots' first three games and only one touchdown pass.
Next up was a daunting trip to the unbeaten Buffalo Bills - led by the 2024 Most Valuable Player Josh Allen - but Maye showed why he narrowly missed out on the MVP award last season, when he led the Patriots to an unexpected Super Bowl run.
After Allen restored Buffalo's lead with a 34-yard touchdown pass to Keon Coleman with four minutes left, Efton Chism made a superb one-handed catch in the endzone to put the Patriots back in front.
They then intercepted a hopeful Allen throw to clinch a 29-26 win, with Maye passing for three touchdowns and 269 yards.
The Bills joined the Rams as Super Bowl favourites last week and they go head to head in LA next week.
Another Eagles injury before London trip
After losing a thriller at Denver last Monday, the LA Rams were 1-2 and faced another stern test on the road this week at the Philadelphia Eagles.
The hosts led 20-10 at half-time after two Darius Cooper touchdowns, but the Rams fought back, with Kyren Williams rushing for two touchdowns in the final four minutes to claim a 24-20 victory.
The fit-again Puka Nacua finished with 125 receiving yards and a touchdown for the Rams, while the Eagles' injury concerns mounted.
Wide receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring) was ruled out before the game, joining tight end Dallas Goedert (knee) on the sidelines, and Philadelphia lost star running back Saquon Barkley to an early hamstring injury.
That is a big blow for the Eagles and UK fans as they visit Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday to face the Jacksonville Jaguars, who beat the Cincinnati Bengals 22-17 to make it back-to-back wins.
The Baltimore Ravens also have fitness concerns over a key man, with two-time MVP Lamar Jackson (ankle) unable to play during the second half of their 24-18 home win against the Tennessee Titans.
Cowboys continue to entertain
There have been at least 48 points in every Dallas Cowboys game this season, and they played their part in another high-scoring affair at state rivals Houston.
The Texans led 23-13 after Nico Collins' second score in the third quarter and then 30-27 with two minutes remaining.
But Dak Prescott led the Cowboys to a game-winning drive of 11 plays and 74 yards, throwing a touchdown pass to star receiver CeeDee Lamb to claim a 34-30 win.
Lamb had a career-high 17 receptions for 189 yards, while team-mate Javonte Williams rushed for three touchdowns as Dallas improved to 2-2.
Sunday's highest scorers were the New York Giants after Jameis Winston, filling in for injured quarterback Jaxson Dart, threw three touchdowns and two interceptions in a 36-24 win at home to the Arizona Cardinals.

552c4b940f1a.text: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is scaling back expectations and zeroing in on a narrowed battlefield as Republicans' prospects of keeping their majority look increasingly bleak. Why it matters: Emmer, a former National Republican Congressional Committee chair who helped the GOP unexpectedly gain seats in 2020, argues his party can still defy historical headwinds in November. But with less than a month to go, Emmer acknowledges that some tough decisions are coming about where Republicans spend their money, including walking away from races they don't think they can salvage. "It really is a business, and you're looking at a balance sheet, and you're putting your money where you're gonna get your biggest return," he told Axios aboard a plane between campaign stops. Axios joined Emmer, who plans to visit 56 districts between September and Election Day, as he traveled from Charlotte to Richmond last week for stops with Reps. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.). Driving the news: It's a lesson Emmer says Republicans learned the hard way in 2022, when expectations of a "red wave" led the party to spread its resources too broadly. "We expanded the map when we should have kept it narrow," Emmer told donors in Charlotte. "We should have been conservative about what we were going after." This cycle, Emmer said Republicans have to identify "where you're not gonna be able to salvage this, and you've got to pick up something over there." Yes, but : That strategy is being tested by a difficult national environment for Republicans, with an unpopular president and voters focused on the cost of living and the war in Iran, which is driving up gas prices. Between the lines: Asked about embattled Rep. Max Miller's (R-Ohio) increasingly difficult race , Emmer immediately pointed up the ticket to the Senate and gubernatorial races, where Democrats are faring better than expected. "The problem is, when you got these statewide candidates that are not creating momentum, that's tough," he said. Emmer also pointed to the North Carolina Senate race, where Democrat Roy Cooper has opened up a lead in polls, as having a "large impact" on the 1st and 11th district races there. Miller has a path to victory, Emmer said, "but it's narrow." Still, he defended the NRCC's decision to spend money backing Miller. Zoom in: Emmer's instinct is to let members run the race that fits their district — within limits. He called Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar's (R-Fla.) campaign ad breaking with Trump on immigration a "huge mistake, adding, "I'm not sure why now was the time for that message" (although he later walked back those comments, saying Salazar "knows her district"). Salazar posited in the ad that Trump's immigration enforcement efforts have "gone too far" and that Hispanic voters who helped elect him in 2024 "feel betrayed."

157fcc6efb4e.text: By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/obama-to-campaign-with-el-sayed-in-detroit-as-ex-president-gets-more-involved-in-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Obama to campaign with El-Sayed in Detroit as ex-president gets more involved in midterms Politics Oct 5, 2026 1:17 PM EDT DETROIT (AP) — Former President Barack Obama will campaign alongside Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit later this month, lending his support to the progressive nominee after a bruising Democratic primary exposed divisions within the party. Obama will appear with El-Sayed at an Oct. 24 rally that will also feature other top Democratic candidates in Michigan, including Jocelyn Benson, the party's nominee for governor. Obama is getting significantly more involved in the midterm elections, with additional campaign stops and advertisements expected to come in the closing weeks, according to plans shared first with The Associated Press. The Detroit event is a notable show of support for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in an August primary and has since worked to consolidate Democratic support in his race against Republican Mike Rogers. The open seat is expected to be among a handful that will decide which party controls the majority next year. Obama taped two dozen ads last week for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate that will be released in the coming days and weeks, in addition to more campaign stops soon to be announced. He appeared earlier this year in a campaign ad with Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek and campaigned in Texas with Senate candidate James Talarico and the candidate for governor, Gina Hinojosa. This week, he will headline a Washington fundraiser supporting Democratic Senate candidates. Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks to attendees at the Carpenters & Millwrights Labor Center during a campaign stop in Warren, Michigan, US, October 3, 2026. Photo by Rebecca Cook/REUTERS Obama aims to help El-Sayed shore up support in a key area El-Sayed defeated Stevens by less than a percentage point in a primary that became a national test of the Democratic Party's ideological direction. El-Sayed drew support from leading progressives, including Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Stevens was backed by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer. Some ads that supported Stevens showed Obama praising her, and she outperformed El-Sayed in Wayne County, winning about 51% of the Democratic primary vote compared with 45% for El-Sayed. The county includes Detroit, where more than three-quarters of residents are Black. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian person to serve as vice president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month. Now the Oct. 24 rally with Obama, the first Black president, could give El-Sayed a boost on the first day of Michigan's required early in-person voting period. Obama spoke with El-Sayed by phone following his primary victory. It will also be a boost for the other candidates in what is one of the most consequential elections in recent Michigan history. There are open races for governor, secretary of state and attorney general, in addition to control of the state legislature being at play. Benson, who will also appear with Obama, is facing Republican Rep. John James in the race for governor. Benson and James are set to debate for the first time on Tuesday, and El-Sayed and Rogers are scheduled to debate for the first time on Oct. 8. WATCH: Harris joins El-Sayed on campaign trail as Democrats focus on Michigan Senate race Obama returns to the campaign trail for the closing stretch Obama has been selective in his involvement in the midterms so far, but his planned ramp-up in the final weeks follows a pattern from recent elections. He campaigned in Detroit on Oct. 22 during the 2024 presidential election and was in the city Oct. 29 during the 2022 midterms. His campaign appearances can draw large crowds and prominent guests. Rapper Eminem introduced Obama at his Detroit rally in 2024. This week, he will headline an event with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee that will include a conversation with Delaware Sen. If a recent hint of dark matter is real, it would rewrite physics. Scientists are already trying to read the outline of that new story’s plot. And that’s reignited interest in certain theories, including a long-beloved but increasingly sidelined concept called supersymmetry.
Dark matter is imperceptibly everywhere, an unidentified type of particle pervading the universe but evident based only on its gravitational effects on galaxies and other cosmic entities. On September 1, scientists with the LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, collaboration announced they’d seen a signal in their detector that could have been caused by a single particle of dark matter — though it could still be just a blip caused by known physics processes.
In the weeks since the detection, dozens of papers have been posted on arXiv.org purporting to explain what LZ saw. Much interest has focused on a theorized type of particle called a higgsino. If the idea is correct, it would be big. “If we discover it, it would be the first discovery of supersymmetry,” says theoretical physicist Harikrishnan Ramani of the University of Delaware in Newark.
Supersymmetry proposes that for each known particle, there exists a heavier counterpart called a superpartner. It’s an idea that could solve multiple physics puzzles at once, so it has attracted a devoted following of physicists.
One of these hypothetical superpartners, such as the higgsino, could be dark matter. The higgsino is the superpartner of the Higgs boson — a particle discovered in 2012 that explains the origin of mass. “If you asked people in the year 2000, ‘What’s your favorite dark matter candidate?’ probably a lot of people would already have said the higgsino then,” says theoretical physicist Tracy Slatyer of MIT.
In recent years, supersymmetry’s popularity has waned, as particle colliders failed to find evidence for it. But as an explanation for LZ’s dark matter hint, a higgsino seems plausible — at least at first glance. “It comes pretty close to working,” Slatyer says.
Physicists spot a puzzling signal
The LZ detector, located at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, S.D., consists of a large tank of liquid xenon. The detector searches for dark matter speeding through the xenon, crashing into it and sending a xenon atomic nucleus zinging away. That’s expected to be a rare event, since dark matter interacts very weakly with normal matter. In the event LZ found, the nucleus recoiled with particularly high energy. Most types of dark matter would produce low-energy recoils in addition to high-energy ones. But LZ didn’t see any low-energy recoils.
If dark matter were a higgsino, that could explain the absence of low-energy events. The higgsino differs from typical dark matter candidates in that it would have two different masses. A collision would happen only if there’s enough energy to bump the higgsino from the lighter to the heavier mass state. That means lower-energy nuclear recoils wouldn’t happen.
Within a day of LZ’s announcement, several papers on the arXiv put forth the higgsino possibility. “I got pretty excited,” says theoretical physicist Katherine Freese of the University of Texas at Austin, a coauthor of one such paper, which was submitted September 1. “First paper I ever wrote in 24 hours.”
But further investigation made the higgsino explanation seem less plausible. For example, if higgsinos exist, they would interact in the sun and get trapped there due to its gravitational pull. There, according to the concepts of supersymmetry, they would annihilate one another and produce high-energy particles called neutrinos. Those neutrinos should have been observed by a neutrino detector located at the South Pole, called IceCube, Ramani and a colleague reported September 2 at arXiv.org. But no such neutrinos have been seen.
And there’s another potential issue. Slatyer and colleagues noticed a plot in an appendix to LZ’s paper that looks at even higher energies. If LZ saw one higgsino at the energy they reported, they’d expect to see even more at these higher energies, the team reported September 3. But LZ didn’t report anything that looked like dark matter at those energies. The LZ detector wasn’t calibrated for those energies, says LZ spokesperson Rick Gaitskell, a physicist at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “We didn’t make any formal claims about detection or even nondetection in that event region,” Gaitskell wrote in a text message. But, if the data are taken seriously, that makes LZ’s event even more difficult to explain with a higgsino.
There’s wiggle room for higgsinos
Considering all these factors makes the higgsino idea a bit of a stretch. But there’s still a little wiggle room. One possibility is that the higgsino’s mass differs from what theoretical physicists expect it to be, about 1,000 times a proton’s mass. That large mass is chosen to allow higgsinos to explain the amount of dark matter seen in the universe today. So changing it complicates the picture, but could make it align better with what LZ saw.
Additional wiggle room comes from the possible speeds of the dark matter particles in the Milky Way. The particles might reach higher velocities than typically assumed, and that could make the data easier to explain. For a faster higgsino to have shown up in LZ, it would require a larger difference in the two masses of the particle. The resulting bigger energy difference means higgsinos have fewer opportunities to produce neutrinos in the sun, explaining why neutrino experiments haven’t seen those particles.
By playing around with those factors, it’s still possible to make the higgsino explanation work, Freese says. Higgsinos with around 2,000 times a proton’s mass could do the trick, Freese and a coauthor report in an October 2 arXiv paper. “Big picture: We love [the] higgsino, and what we’re doing now is putting in the details that we think are important,” she says.

b3bd12782ada.text: By — Stephen Whyno, Associated Press Stephen Whyno, Associated Press By — Noah Trister, Associated Press Noah Trister, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/washington-capitals-captain-alex-ovechkin-says-hell-retire-at-the-end-of-his-22nd-season Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Washington Capitals captain Alex Ovechkin says he'll retire at the end of his 22nd season Nation Oct 5, 2026 12:55 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Alex Ovechkin said Monday that his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captain who holds the league's career goal-scoring record. Ovechkin addressed teammates to deliver the news before the team posted a message from him on social media. WATCH: Alex Ovechkin breaks Gretzky's record to become NHL's all-time leading goal scorer "It's sad, but it is what it is," Ovechkin said in his locker room address. "It's hard, but let's enjoy it and let's do some special things this year." Ovechkin signed a one-year contract this past summer and turned 41 on Sept. 17. All signs pointed to this being the end, and he said he and his family decided as much in recent months. "I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it's the right decision," the Russian star said in a statement released before the Capitals' home opener Wednesday night. Ovechkin broke Wayne Gretzky's goals record in April 2025 and entered this season at 929. The front office acquired Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch in trades and signed fellow forward Boone Jenner and defenseman Vincent Desharnais in free agency to add around a young core in the hopes of making another long playoff run and contending for the Stanley Cup. "Let's make the playoffs, let's have fun and enjoy the moment because times fly," Ovechkin told the team. "For young guys who are first year or experienced guys, I remember that moment, and enjoy the time. Because times fly. It seems like yesterday I was here my first year." Speaking to reporters later Monday, Ovechkin said this was the right time to announce his decision, two days before the home opener. "I'm not 20 years old," he said. "I want to play with my kids when they're growing up. Play hockey, play soccer, play basketball. I want to be healthy enough to do that kind of stuff." Ovechkin has spent his entire career with Washington, winning the Calder Trophy as rookie of the year in 2005-06, the Hart Trophy as MVP three times and leading the NHL in scoring nine times. He was playoff MVP in 2018 when he led the Caps to the first Stanley Cup championship in franchise history. Washington Capitals left wing Alex Ovechkin (8) hoists the Stanley Cup after defeating the Vegas Golden Knights in game five of the 2018 Stanley Cup Final at T-Mobile Arena,Jun 7, 2018; Las Vegas. Photo by Stephen R. Sylvanie / Reuters/ USA TODAY Sports There's been speculation Ovechkin could receive an unfriendly reception on the road after he appeared in an ad for a party aligned with Vladimir Putin during the offseason. But there wasn't much sign of that during the first two games of the season — at Carolina and at Tampa Bay. When addressing the fallout from that last month, Ovechkin confirmed he'd be going back to live in Russia when he retired from the NHL. In Washington's season-opening win over the Hurricanes, Ovechkin had 12 minutes, 46 seconds of ice time, the lowest of his career in a game when he wasn't injured or ejected. Monday was 21 years to the day after Ovechkin made his debut with the Capitals. "It's been pretty good career, pretty good 22 seasons," he said. "Obviously the goal that we have, to bring a Stanley Cup to D.C., we did it." Although the Capitals have designs on making the playoffs this season, within a couple hours of Ovechkin's announcement, tickets for Washington's regular-season home finale against Pittsburgh on April 4 were going for a minimum of $825 on StubHub. With D.C. hosting college hockey's Frozen Four next year, the Capitals finish the regular season with three straight road games, wrapping up April 10 at Philadelphia. The Capitals missed the playoffs in 2025-26, but Ovechkin played all 82 games and scored 32 goals. He's reached 30 in every season of his career except 2020-21, when he played only 45 games. Long before he broke through during the Capitals' Stanley Cup run, Ovechkin had rejuvenated hockey in Washington, and he'll retire as one of the city's most accomplished athletes in any sport. The Capitals drafted him No. 1 overall in 2004, and he and Pittsburgh's Sidney Crosby became stars almost immediately in 2005 when the league emerged from missing a season because of a lockout. FILE PHOTO: National Hockey League number one draft Alexander Ovechkin of Moscow, Russia puts on a Washington Capitals sweater after being picked at the in Raleigh, North Carolina June 26, 2004. Photo by Ellen Ozier/ Reuters/ TLC/JDP Ovechkin's combination of goal-scoring skill, physicality and boundless energy made him an instant hit, and he scored a career-high 65 goals in his third season, which earned him the first of his Hart Trophies. Washington's penchant for postseason heartache, which existed long before Ovechkin showed up, followed him for a while as well. The Capitals won the Presidents' Trophy three times with the league's best regular-season record, falling short in the playoffs each time before a Washington team that merely won its division finally went all the way in the playoffs. In four postseason meetings between Crosby and Ovechkin — in 2009, 2016, 2017, 2018 — the winner won the Stanley Cup each time. Washington's home opener Wednesday is against Pittsburgh. 5d56c661dfe2.text: By — Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/floridas-dengue-outbreak-is-largest-in-continental-u-s-in-decades Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Florida's dengue outbreak is largest in continental U.S. in decades Science Oct 5, 2026 2:35 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Florida's current dengue outbreak appears to be the largest in several decades in the continental United States. State health officials reported this week that more than 250 locally acquired cases of the mosquito-borne disease have been tallied so far this year. The vast majority of them were in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Federal health officials say their data on dengue outbreaks is limited. But available information from state health departments and medical journals suggests the Florida outbreak marks the most cases in a calendar year for any state since at least the 1940s. Puerto Rico is consistently hit hard by dengue, with numbers much higher than what's seen in any of the 50 states. But in the continental U.S., Florida usually gets the most locally transmitted cases. The state's previous worst year was 2023, when just under 200 locally spread cases were reported. Officials in Hillsborough and surrounding counties have declared local emergencies, and workers in the Tampa area are spraying day and night to tamp down the population of disease-transmitting mosquitoes. What is dengue? Dengue (pronounced DEHN'-gay) is caused by a virus spread by a type of mosquito. Many infected people don't get sick, but some experience fever, flu-like symptoms and — notoriously — aches. It's been nicknamed "breakbone fever" for the excruciating pain some people experience. Severe cases can cause bleeding, shock and death. There has been one dengue death in Florida this year — an elderly Tampa woman on Sept. 4. There are four types of dengue virus, simply known as 1, 2, 3 and 4. When someone is first infected, their body builds antibodies against that type for life. If they get infected with another type of dengue, the antibodies from the first infection may fail to neutralize the second type — and actually can help the virus enter immune cells and replicate. That's made it difficult to develop an effective vaccine. Most people in the Tampa area don't have prior immunity to any form of dengue, said Dawn Wesson, a Tulane University expert on dengue and other diseases spread by mosquitoes. How does dengue spread? The warm-weather mosquitoes that spread dengue live in Florida and some other hotter U.S. locales, but experts say they have been expanding their geographic reach because of climate change. For decades, most continental U.S. infections were found among people who caught the virus while traveling internationally, along with locally acquired cases in Puerto Rico. But in 2009-2010, Key West, Florida, reported the first dengue cases acquired in the continental U.S. outside of the Texas-Mexico border since 1945. WATCH: Scientists explore new ways to target mosquitoes as warming climate expands threat The largest outbreak of dengue in any U.S. state since then occurred in Hawaii, where 264 locally acquired cases were reported over a six-month span in 2015-2016. The Tampa-area outbreak, which first came to light in July, is already on the verge of surpassing that. Across the world, more than 2.2 million infections and nearly 1,200 deaths have been reported this year, according to the World Health Organization. There have been nearly 1,900 locally acquired U.S. cases this year, most of them in Puerto Rico, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Why is it so bad in Tampa? Florida tends to get a lot of dengue in part because the state receives a lot of travelers who have been to Puerto Rico or other places where the disease is present, Wesson said. Usually most cases are in southern Florida, around the Miami area. It's hard to say what's happening in the Tampa area this year, but the surge may be at least partly related to travel patterns, she added. Locally acquired cases in Florida have actually surpassed travel-associated cases, by a count of 252 to 245 as of last week. But it's close, and at least 13 Hillsborough County cases were diagnosed in travelers, according to the state. Traditionally, the CDC would be highly visible in a situation like this, but it hasn't been this time, Wesson noted. The U.S. public health agency has to be invited in by state officials, however, and Florida officials have not asked for CDC disease investigators to come in, CDC spokesman Jason McDonald said. The agency has provided $800,000 in assistance to the state health department, he added. What can you do to prevent infection? The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed. People in an outbreak area can take their own steps for protection, experts say. The virus-carrying mosquitoes can bite any time of day, so it's important for people in an outbreak area to apply EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients like DEET, experts say. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants to cover the skin and make it harder for mosquitoes to bite. Staying indoors, behind screens or in rooms with air conditioning will also lessen the chances for a bite. Those steps are especially important just after sunrise and around sunset, when mosquitoes tend to be most active, researchers say. People should also check their property and get rid of any pooled water where mosquitoes might breed. Climate conditions and persistent mosquito populations will likely make local dengue outbreaks a more frequent problem, Wesson said. "There's a good chance that this is the new normal," she said. 3d2335261f39.text: By — Ahmed Al-Haj, Associated Press Ahmed Al-Haj, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/saudi-backed-coalition-forces-houthis-from-several-areas-around-key-strait-yemeni-officials-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Saudi-backed coalition forces Houthis from several areas around key strait, Yemeni officials say World Oct 5, 2026 2:28 PM EDT ADEN, Yemen (AP) — Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said Monday. The officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government have retaken the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns. The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under air cover by a Saudi military coalition. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, Rubio said that Saudi Arabia and the U.S. have a defense agreement but wouldn't offer more details. The Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis have come under attack, and "they have a right to defend themselves," Rubio said. The U.S. has provided support to Saudi Arabia in its ongoing campaign against the Houthis, according to a regional official and a U.S. official. This U.S. support included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the offensive, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to reporters. The U.S. had supported the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis early in the Yemen war, before quitting the coalition in recent years. The offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the southwestern part of Yemen, taking a key town in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward a strategic provincial capital in the region. The Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition has secured "air protection" of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign. The air campaign follows the fall of a key town in Yemen The Houthi rebels seized the town of Turbah on Sunday, shortly before the internationally recognized government announced a major military operation against them. The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire. Turbah sits on a main road linking the provincial capital of Taiz with the port city of Aden, which serves as an interim seat of Yemen's government. Over the years, the town was a major post for the government forces defending Taiz against the Houthis. Earlier, the Houthis seized several villages and areas on Taiz's outskirts in a series of advances, paving the way for the rebels to encircle Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city. Yemen's flare-up shows the capabilities of the Iran-backed rebels The Houthis made a swift push on the country's western coast on the Red Sea in early September. They captured the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that enabled them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial chokepoint through which 12% of global trade transits. In its announcement Sunday, the Saudi-backed government said it was mobilizing troops across government-held areas. Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operations were aiming at "recovering the remaining territories" controlled by the Houthis. He called on the international community to provide support to his government. READ MORE: Iran-backed Houthi rebels warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's growing civil war Hours after al-Alimi's declaration, the Saudi military spokesperson al-Malki vowed "full operational support" to the Yemeni government forces, until the Houthis are "eliminated." Al-Malki also stressed Saudi Arabia's right to take all necessary measures to deter the rebels who continued to fire missiles and drones at the kingdom as part of the nearly three-month escalation that revived Yemen's civil war. Saudi-backed government forces are trying to fight back Al-Alimi said in a post on X on Monday that the operation — dubbed "Yemen Dawn" — has started with the aim of "restoring state institutions, liberating" Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-controlled capital, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup." Al-Nazili said government forces were carrying out a "strategic offensive" on Sanaa. The Houthi media office reported multiple airstrikes by the Saudi coalition on their territories, including Sanaa. The latest flare-up began in mid-July, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing the airport in Sanaa to prevent the landing of an unauthorized Iranian flight. The rebels responded with missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces in the country. They also announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and attacked several Saudi-linked vessels. Then in September, they intensified their campaign, storming down the Red Sea coast in their biggest land grab in years. aee05747004a.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/after-redistricting-a-black-community-in-louisiana-faces-a-future-without-a-champion-in-congress Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter After redistricting, a Black community in Louisiana faces a future without a champion in Congress Politics Oct 5, 2026 2:06 PM EDT SCOTLANDVILLE, La. (AP) — If you cross the Mississippi River on the Huey P. Long-O.K. Allen Bridge, pass the Exxon Refinery, then head north for a few minutes, you'll find a pocket of Louisiana that's unlike any other place in America's never-ending battle over what it means to have equal representation. Here is Scotlandville, which was once its own unincorporated town but is now part of Baton Rouge. It's a nearly all Black community of 10,000 people that has been, for the second time, shuffled around on the state's congressional map to make it part of a majority white district. Both times it was during the term of the same representative. The first time was 1996, when a group of voters sued to redraw the lines. The second time was earlier this year, after the U.S. Supreme Court decided that a core part of the Voting Rights Act intended to protect minorities' political rights was unconstitutional. The ruling led to cascading changes around the American South, but the case originated in Louisiana — specifically the 6th Congressional District that included Scotlandville. This is where Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields, 63, grew up poor and attended local schools before graduating from nearby Southern University A&M, eventually climbing the ranks to the U.S. House. Now he plans to leave Washington and return to the Legislature instead of running for reelection in a race that he sees little chance of winning because the district boundaries have been altered dramatically. Scotlandville will no longer be represented by a native son, someone who people believed instinctively understood their challenges and offered a direct line to power and influence in the nation's capital. "We're back to where we were right after Reconstruction," said Press Robinson Sr., 89, who has spent years working on issues involving the congressional map. "When they redistrict, they are not concerned about the effect it has on those of us who are people of color." The methods have changed over the years, he said, but the intent has not. "They disenfranchise people of color and they've done it again," Robinson said. Field's career echoes legal battle for representation Congressional districts are core to debates over racial equality in the South, where white leaders spent decades using gerrymandering to ensure Black people couldn't gain enough power to elect their own representatives. The Voting Rights Act signed by Democratic President Lyndon Johnson in 1965 was supposed to fix that. Among other things, it required states and jurisdictions with a history of racial discrimination to get approval from the U.S. Department of Justice before congressional maps could take effect. It also allowed people to sue to challenge laws and procedures that would deny them the chance to elect candidates of their choice. That didn't settle the issue, however, and there has been a series of legal battles since then. Fields' political career has tracked those twists and turns over the years. He first came to Congress in 1993 when Scotlandville was part of the 4th District, which had been redrawn to create a majority Black seat. A federal court said in 1996 the boundaries that zigzagged from northwest portion of the state to the Baton Rouge area were unconstitutional. Scotlandville shifted to the 6th District, which was then predominantly white, and Fields became a state senator. But he had an opening to return to Washington when Robinson and other plaintiffs challenged how the state drew its maps following the 2020 census. WATCH: How the Supreme Court's Louisiana districting decision weakens the Voting Rights Act A 2023 court decision involving Alabama also affected Louisiana, requiring the state to draw new district lines to achieve fairer representation for minorities. The district became majority Black again, and Fields won the seat in 2024. Another wave of litigation was already starting, and the issue soon reached the U.S. Supreme Court once more. The new lawsuit by a group of non-Black voters dovetailed with a separate effort by President Donald Trump to push Republican-led states to redraw their maps to help his party keep control of Congress in this year's midterms. The high court's conservative majority said Fields' district was unconstitutional. Louisiana, Alabama and Tennessee raced to redo their U.S. House districts in time for the November elections. In Alabama, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figueres is fighting to hold onto his seat, where Black voting age population dropped from 50% to 40% under the new political lines, according to an Associated Press analysis of the citizen voting age population in his redrawn district. In Tennessee, the majority Black district anchored by Memphis was split between three others. Fields' district went from being 53% Black to 25% in the new one. He announced in July that he wasn't going to run for reelection. Blocks from the main entrance to Southern University A&M, a small crowd hung around a convenience store, but people were unwilling to talk about politics, eyeing strangers suspiciously. One younger man said he didn't know who represents the area on the city council, let alone in Congress. Frank Levy, 56, the cashier, said people's apathy created the political environment that allowed for gerrymandering to occur again. "A lot of people don't even think about politics like this," he said. "They don't understand." 3871336bb8c4.text: By — Maurico Savarese, Associated Press Maurico Savarese, Associated Press By — Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/lula-shake-ups-campaign-as-flavio-bolsonaro-reaches-for-more-support-ahead-of-brazils-runoff Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lula shake-ups campaign as Flávio Bolsonaro reaches for more support ahead of Brazil's runoff World Oct 5, 2026 1:43 PM EDT BRASILIA, Brazil (AP) — Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, an ally of President Donald Trump, has pulled off a surprisingly strong showing in Brazil's first round of presidential elections, giving him momentum in the weeks before an Oct. 25 runoff against incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, has allied himself with the Trump administration at a moment when Trump allies are taking power in Latin America, while Lula has spoken out against U.S. interference in the Brazilian elections and built a stronger relationship with Beijing. In a tight race on Sunday, Bolsonaro garnered 47% of the vote to the populist leftist president's 45%. Since neither candidate secured an absolute majority, they will face off again in three weeks. The winner of Brazil's first round of voting has never lost an election, though never before has the second-place candidate been so close in the results. Here's what to know about the upcoming second round and what it means for Brazil. Candidates are preparing strategies for a tight race The 80-year-old Lula will face an uphill battle to win the presidency for the fourth nonconsecutive term, analysts say. Edinho Silva, the chairman of Lula's Workers' Party, told journalists in Sao Paulo that the president will meet with campaign managers in Brasilia seeking to refine his message delivery, evaluate regional turnout figures, and re-allocate resources to key battleground states ahead of the second round. TV debates, which were snubbed by both candidates in the first round, will also be key, he said. "Now it is mano a mano. We will show Brazilians that Flávio Bolsonaro is dangerous and will not run this country in a way they will see their lives improve," Silva said. "We will try to speak to every democratic force in this country." READ MORE: Bolsonaro and Lula head to a runoff in Brazil's presidential election On the opposition side, Bolsonaro is engaging in outreach to political figures, party leaders and regional allies to consolidate support. His team is focusing on building on his already impressive congressional backing: His Liberal Party won more than one-third of the Senate on Sunday — which is unusual in Brazil's fractured political system. Three of the other 10 presidential candidates from the first round have said they will not endorse either candidate. Lula faces a spirit of change with Brazil's right-wing Lula is fighting a trend of frustration with incumbents and a shift to the right in Brazil and worldwide, according to Creomar de Souza, a political analyst with Dharma Political Risk and Strategy, a political consultancy firm based in Brasilia. "The spirit of the times is pushing Brazil to another place. Since 2016, Brazil is under that right-wing spirit. It leaned to Flávio this time, but it could have been anybody else on the right," de Souza said. "It will be tough for Lula to win. He is rowing from the back when he thought by now they would be winning by a small margin. Can he do it? Yes. Is it likely? It will be very tough." Tom Ferreira, 35, a business administrator who has voted for Lula in past elections, is an example of a former Lula voter who swung to Bolsonaro. He cast his ballot for Bolsonaro this time, although he preferred the proposals of some of the other candidates who didn't get many votes, like Romeu Zema and Ronaldo Caiado. He doesn't think Bolsonaro has strong proposals. "It's more of a question of change," he said. "Today, people vote in a way that's like, 'I'm for Bolsonaro,' or 'I'm for Lula.' ... Nobody votes because they researched the candidate or saw what they've done." The shuttered Banco Master corruption scandal that exposed Bolsonaro had accepted millions of dollars from disgraced banker, Daniel Vorcaro, to fund a movie about his father's life wasn't a deal-breaker for Ferreira because he believes most politicians are corrupt. "They bring Bolsonaro into it, but really everyone's involved," he said. Some voters give some hope to Lula, too. Brenda Alves de Carvalho, a 27-year-old financial assistant, voted for another presidential candidate, Augusto Cury, in the first round but says she will support Lula in the runoff. That doesn't mean she is excited about it. She said that the president's third term was not great, but it is "closer to what we want." "I didn't want to vote at first. I know now I'll have to vote for one side, because I don't want to cast a blank vote." Savarese reported from Sao Paulo. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 170b9fc8efe7.text: By — Hillel Italie, Associated Press Hillel Italie, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-francis-diaries-to-be-published-next-month-revealing-reflections-on-vatican-years Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Francis' diaries to be published next month, revealing reflections on Vatican years World Oct 5, 2026 1:33 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Journal entries kept by Pope Francis before and during his papacy will be published this fall for the first time. Image, an imprint of Penguin Random House Christian Publishing Group, announced Monday that "The Private Diary of Pope Francis" will be released in English and four other languages on Nov. 24. According to Image, the book will provide an "extraordinary glimpse" into the late pontiff's "hopes and fears, struggles and prayers." It will be issued in partnership with Libreria Editrice Vaticana, or LEV, the Vatican Publishing House. The writings span from December 1992, just over two decades before he became pope, to August 2024, eight months before he died and was succeeded by Pope Leo XIV. The English-language edition of his private reflections was translated from the Spanish original by Sister Bernadette Reis and edited and annotated by Víctor Manuel Fernández, an Argentine cardinal who heads the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. READ MORE: Pope Leo meets LGBTQ+ Catholic advocate and vows continuity with Pope Francis' legacy of welcome Born Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Francis was a native of Argentina and history's first Latin American pope. He was known for his down-to-earth style and emphasis on humility, including visits to poor countries with persecuted Christian minorities rather than the traditional strongholds of Catholicism. At the start of the coronavirus pandemic, from an empty St. Peter's Square, he called for "all of us to row together, each of us in need of comforting the other." At times, he was controversial. He angered some conservatives with his outreach to LGBTQ+ Catholics and was widely criticized for saying that those who accused Chilean Bishop Juan Barros of helping to protect the alleged pedophile Rev. Fernando Karadima had committed slander. In 2016, commenting on then-presidential candidate Donald Trump's vow to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexican border, Francis said that anyone building a wall to keep migrants out "is not Christian." In his lifetime, Francis' books included "The Name of God Is Mercy" and the memoir "Hope." He died on April 21, 2025 at the age of 88. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 4a2beec114f0.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Katie Marie Davies, Associated Press Katie Marie Davies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ukraine-claims-its-strikes-have-taken-out-more-than-half-of-russias-oil-refining-capacity Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ukraine claims its strikes have taken out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity World Oct 5, 2026 1:29 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine says its long-range strikes have neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces during its 4 1/2-year-old invasion. The Defense Ministry said late Sunday that recent strikes on refineries in cities, including Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran, had disabled 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified. Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their aerial assaults as progress along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line has largely ground to a halt. Ukrainian strikes cause fuel issues in Russia Ukraine has launched repeated attacks on refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict gasoline sales. Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country's oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes' economic impact, President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. "They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially," Putin told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said analysts from Ukraine's intelligence services, the General Staff and the Defense Ministry had assessed the strikes' effects. "Fifty-one percent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy's economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings. Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory," he said. Russia has historically been the world's third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude, after the U.S. and China. Some of Russia's 32 refineries have been hit as many as 15 times since the start of the war, and one refinery has been hit every three days in recent months, creating a cycle of damage and emergency repairs that could degrade units long term, according to the International Energy Agency. Ukrainian strikes have also increasingly targeted the more complex equipment that removes impurities from fuel, which takes months to repair. The IEA says diesel output has fallen by about 30%, and drivers have had to wait up to 40 hours to fill up at gasoline stations. Russian refiners have tried to compensate by delaying scheduled maintenance and bringing mothballed units back online. Another response has been to lower fuel quality standards to maintain gasoline supplies, which risks damage to engines and pollution control equipment. The Kremlin has also banned diesel exports, pushing global prices higher and prompting U.S. President Donald Trump on Sept. 13 to urge Ukraine to stop hitting refineries. "There may be people under the rubble of the residential building that was hit. A search and rescue operation is underway," Terekhov wrote on his Telegram channel. An earlier Russian drone attack on the city's Industrialnyi district also killed one person, Terekhov said late Sunday. Vehicles and an administrative building were set alight and apartment buildings were damaged, he said. Another person was also killed in a separate Russian attack on the Sloviansk community in Ukraine's Donetsk region, said Vadym Liakh, head of the Sloviansk city military administration. He urged residents not to wait for a mandatory evacuation order but to leave the area. Russia's Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that it had struck an electrical substation in the Kharkiv region, in addition to energy and port infrastructure and maritime vessels used by Ukraine's military elsewhere in the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone attack caused a fire on board a commercial vessel that later sank in the Black Sea. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy described the attack as "a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel" in neutral waters. He said the vessel was Turkish-owned and carrying corn. Russia did not immediately comment on the incident. Ukraine has struggled in recent weeks to fend off Russia's intensified aerial attacks on cities that include ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones. Kyiv has suffered under repeated air raid alerts, punctuated by loud explosions from drone and missile strikes. The onslaught aims to terrorize civilians, officials and analysts say, and break their will to resist Russia's full-scale invasion since 2022. President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.
Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
So urgent had the departure been that some of the planes left before refuelling aircraft could be arranged to support them, US officials who wished to remain anonymous told the New York Times.
"So, what you saw there is the secretary of war [Pete Hegseth], out of an abundance of caution, trying to protect our guys," Vice-President JD Vance said as he left Washington for a trip to Alaska.
Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.
Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.
"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."
Washington, he added, "actually knows the people that made the threat", he but did not confirm who.
The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.
One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.
"Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.
Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.
He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.
Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, was quoted as saying by Reuters news agency.
However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added.
The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education.
It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested.
One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week.
France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale LycÃ©enne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete".
The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement".
Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest.
The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.
The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers.
The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu announced a series of measures to "address the difficulties faced by secondary school students and education staff", promising "visible changes" in schools.
However, he also said: "We will make no concessions to violence. We stand by students and staff who have been assaulted, as well as police officers and gendarmes who have been injured."
The unrest has not only seen schools blockaded, but also rubbish bins set on fire. Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "burned and ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Violent clashes between students and the police have led to some serious injuries throughout the course of the protests so far.
On Monday, a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation near a school in the northern city of Lens. The student was transferred to a nearby hospital and his injury is not life-threatening, according to officials.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'AumÃ´ne after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."
Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry, external.
Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors.
The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner".
While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised.
The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand.
The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response.
"This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.
Meanwhile MÃ©lenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations".
The left-wing mayor of Marseille, BenoÃ®t Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said.

Armed Border Patrol agents raided a protest camp in Lochiel, in southeast Arizona, making way for contractors to cut down the last standing cottonwood tree Monday morning for a double border wall, after protesters protected it for more than 70 days.
Activists in Lochiel said at least 12 people had been arrested as of 8 a.m. during the ongoing raid. Border Patrol agents ignored demands for a warrant as they entered the private property and destroyed tents, according to news releases from activist groups on the ground.
Dubbed the “grandmother tree,” the cottonwood cut down Monday was hundreds of years old. It was one of several that lined the edge of private property along Border Road, a dirt road that runs along the U.S.-Mexico border, in a remote area of Arizona in the San Rafael Valley about 25 miles east of Nogales.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection said Monday in a statement to Arizona Luminaria that it has now removed all four cottonwood trees on federal land in Lochiel that were marked for removal.
“CBP recognizes the importance of protecting the environment, wildlife, and cultural resources during border wall construction,” the statement said. “While concerns exist about impacts to sensitive areas, it is important to note that illegal immigration itself poses significant environmental challenges. High volumes of unauthorized crossings often result in substantial amounts of trash, pollution, and damage to natural resources, including sensitive habitats and agriculture.”
CBP did not answer additional questions from Arizona Luminaria about how many protesters were arrested or what charges they face.
After three cottonwoods were cut down in June, activists set up a tree-sit in an attempt to protect the last remaining grandmother tree. At least one person sat or slept in the tree at all times. For 71 days, people camped out in private property just north of the tree and took turns occupying it.
On Monday around 6:30 a.m., Border Patrol agents with their faces covered began to arrest protesters, videos posted on Instagram show. People screamed and some warned the agents that they were pushing people into barbed wire on the ground. The protesters were trying to move back onto the private property on the other side of the barbed wire.
“You’re stepping on them!” a person is heard screaming.
“You’re pushing them into barbed wire!” someone else yells at the agents.
Another video shot from a distance shows the giant tree falling over as people scream and cry.
Life at the Camp
Kate Scott, co-founder of Madrean Archipelago Wildlife Center, was the first to notice contractors were cutting down the cottonwoods this summer. After speaking to a worker in June, and learning their plans to cut down all the trees, she gathered support and started sitting out near the tree. Eventually, with the support of Indigenous activists, the protesters in Lochiel started a morning prayer ritual. Every morning the group would hold a sunrise prayer for the land, Scott said. It was during that prayer ceremony that Border Patrol agents raided the camp on Monday.
When Arizona Luminaria visited the camp on Sept. 23, it was a quiet day at the protest camp, with only one or two Border Patrol vehicles driving through the area. As of late morning, there was no construction happening near the camp. But months earlier, when the protest first started, construction workers would arrive around 3 a.m. and work all morning, Scott said.
“This was a very, very intense place,” she said, adding that the sound of the machinery would wake them in the early hours.
About a quarter mile east of where the tree once stood, two rows of 30-foot tall border panels on either side of the road came to a sudden stop. A stack of panels on the road sat between the two walls and another stack of panels sat a few feet away. The new wall runs east along the rolling hills in this area of the border as far as the eye can see.
On Sept. 14, three protesters wearing bird and jaguar costumes, representing the endangered species in the area, were arrested after entering the construction site.Those arrests encouraged more people from across the country to join the camp, Scott said.
In late September, dozens of tents were scattered along the tall grass inside private property. A group of people were learning to safely climb rope to get onto the wooden plank in the grandmother tree.
Down the road, the group had secured a guest house with a bathroom, a bed and fridges to store food and other belongings. The landowner was renting it out to the group. Scott called it “Casita de la Esperanza,” meaning House of Hope.
Another cottonwood, this one in Mexico, held banners that read, “From MN to MX resistance is fertile,” and “Chinga la Migra.” Four calves rested in the shade inside a pen. For about a week, activists in Mexico held their own tree sit in solidarity with U.S. protesters.
To get to Lochiel, a visitor has to traverse more than 10 miles of rough dirt roads through the Coronado National Forest. It’s a remote ranching town between Nogales and Bisbee, south of Sonoita. Ranch homes are scattered on vast parcels of land. A small white church sits about 100 feet from the border wall, with a large white cross standing on a hill above the church. Where there aren’t 30-foot border panels, a barbed-wire fence about 3 to 4 feet tall marks the border.
Along Border Road, between Casita de la Esperanza and where the last remaining grandmother tree once stood, the trunks of two other cottonwoods lay on the ground after being cut down. There was a third between them, Scott said, but it was dragged up the hill to a “graveyard of grandmothers.”
The two fallen trees were so big they left a 4 foot deep hole in the ground where they were once rooted. Banners activists tied around the trunk remain on the fallen trees. And on one of them, new growth had started to come up, with bright green leaves emerging from the trunk.
This article first appeared on AZ Luminaria and is republish

The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments from oil companies on Monday that could help decide the fate of more than two dozen lawsuits accusing the industry of deceiving the public about climate change. The claims seek potentially billions of dollars in damages to help pay the costs imposed by climate-related extreme weather.
Yet the questions before the court did not focus on the merits of these claims but instead on technical legal matters over whether they should proceed at all.
The case being argued was brought in 2018 by the city and county of Boulder against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy in Colorado state court. While the case and dozens like it have survived multiple appeals in state and federal courts, the oil companies are asking the Supreme Court to declare that federal law preempts state and local governments from bringing such claims.
“This case represents an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct,” said Kannon Shanmugam, arguing for Exxon and Suncor. In effect, Shanmugam said, Boulder is attempting to use state law to regulate oil company activity around the world. “If Boulder’s claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country would have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil fuel producers.”
But Boulder and dozens of other plaintiffs have argued their claims do not attempt to impose any limits on oil companies at all—the Boulder case seeks damages, not an injunction on any activity.
“This case is not about emissions,” said Kevin Russell, who argued the case for Boulder. “It’s about deception.”
Oil companies and conservative groups have been ramping up a campaign to block the lawsuits from proceeding as they inch closer to trial. Some states have enacted laws barring such lawsuits and Republicans have introduced federal legislation that would shield oil companies from climate liability claims. The Trump administration has also intervened in several state cases, including Boulder’s, to try to block them from moving forward. Many scientists whose work is being cited in the cases have been the subject of more than 100 public records requests from conservative groups seeking information about their work and funders, according to Politico.
The first question that arose at Monday’s hearing, posed by Justice Clarence Thomas, is whether the court has jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage because no ruling has been issued.
The oil companies contend that the proliferating lawsuits are already causing sufficient harm and that the court should decide now whether the cases should proceed. Several justices suggested they thought it might be too early to intervene.
“I think Boulder’s best shot is on the jurisdictional question, whether this case is too early,” Michael Gerrard, faculty director at the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University, said in an interview.
The justices also probed the arguments of whether federal law preempts a state claim about climate change and emissions, either through the Clean Air Act or the Constitution.
Several of the conservative justices seemed inclined to agree that federal law preempts at least some of Boulder’s claims, Gerrard said.

The oil companies’ lawyers have argued that the Clean Air Act preempts any claims against oil companies tied to climate pollution. They also argue that the Constitution itself gives the federal government exclusive control over interstate pollution.
Russell argued that Boulder’s claim does not seek to limit pollution, and that there is nothing in the Clean Air Act or the Constitution that would bar states from taking actions that have a secondary effect of reducing pollution, such as imposing a gas tax or, in this case, seeking damages from oil companies.
Justice Samuel Alito was not at the hearing after recusing himself last week. While Alito gave no explanation for the decision, he had been under pressure to do so because he owns stock in oil companies that are party to other lawsuits that would be affected by the court’s decision.
Alito’s absence leaves open the possibility of a tie vote, which would allow the case to move forward.
Supporters of the case held rallies outside the court calling on the justices to let it proceed.
“Boulder, like other cities and counties across the country, is confronting realities associated with climate change every day, from wildfires and floods to drought, extreme heat, and growing pressures on our water and infrastructure,” said Boulder’s city manager, Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde, in a statement after the hearing. “The legal question before the court is whether taxpayers must bear these costs alone or must the defendants also pay their fair share for the harms they have caused.”
Many conservative groups and politicians have filed briefs supporting the oil companies, and the Trump administration presented arguments to the justices on Monday.
Boulder won supportive briefs from not only climate advocacy groups and Democrats but also many academics and former Environmental Protection Agency officials, including some appointed by Republican presidents.
Many of the cases brought by states and local governments have been paused pending the outcome of the Supreme Court’s ruling in the Boulder case. The decision, expected by the end of the court’s term in June, could bring those claims to an abrupt halt or set the stage for trials to finally begin.
