A US man who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for murdering his wife.
Caleb Flynn, 40, was found guilty last week after a short deliberation by the jury, which rejected his claim that an intruder broke into his Ohio home and shot his wife, Ashley Flynn, as she slept.
He was also found guilty of eight additional charges, including aggravated murder and tampering with evidence.
Letters from his two daughters were read in court during the sentencing hearing on Monday, pleading with him to finally admit his guilt and questioning why he killed their mother.
Flynn, a former music pastor, fatally shot his wife, a 37-year-old teacher, in February before staging their home in Tipp City to appear as if someone had broken in through the garage.
Flynn claims he was asleep when he heard gunshots and found his wife dead in bed after finding the garage door open. Their two children, ages 9 and 11, were also sleeping in the house at the time.
His wife's sister, Kayla Keyt, read a victim impact statement saying the murder had caused his daughters to question their Christian faith and had "shattered a family who trusted you".
One of his daughter's letters read: "Dear Daddy, I don't even know where to start. How could you do such a thing?"
She also said: "Mommy was the perfect person... And then you chose to kill the only mother I ever had."
The other daughter's letter began "Dear Caleb", rather than addressing him as her father, and asked him to "tell everyone what you did it and receive your outcome".
"You made me feel like an idiot thinking I could trust you," his daughter said. She added that she continues to have faith in God, and that she will never visit her father in prison.
Flynn sobbed loudly as the letters from his children were read.
The sentencing hearing also included Flynn reading a statement expressing love for his family, apologising for unspecified "decisions" that he made, and again claiming that he did not kill his wife.
"I made vows to Ashley on our wedding day. I failed those vows," he said.
Judge Jeannine Pratt called Flynn an "extreme" risk to the public as she imposed her sentence.
The murder verdict last week followed eight days of testimony, during which several incriminating text messages Flynn sent to his former mistress, Alleigha Botner, were read out and AI-generated songs were played that prosecutors said he made for her.
Evidence presented during trial included police body camera footage and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch from around the time of the murder when he claimed to have been sleeping.
The prosecution also called dozens of witnesses, including Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church.
Botner read aloud in court some of their 100,000 text messages, including one where Flynn wrote: "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail."
In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone."
Flynn did not testify during the trial, and his defence team called no witnesses.
His lawyer, Patrick Mulligan, has said he plans to file a notice of appeal, telling reporters last week: "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design."
Mulligan argued that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder and questioned why Flynn was being accused of tampering with evidence because his gun could not be found.
This gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open.
Prosecutor Paul Watkins read a statement from Ashley Flynn's family in court after the verdict in September, saying: "Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart."
"She loved people," the statement continued. "Most of all, she loved being a Mum."
Flynn briefly appeared on American Idol in 2013, saying that he loved his wife "more than anything".

f6e29287ac6d.text: President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague , though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it. Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began. Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution. Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work. No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported. What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger." The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance , but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert. The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak. Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID

The Scoop
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York has been visiting big banks to review their loans to private credit firms and understand their exposure to a financial industry that has unnerved investors and global policymakers.
Fed officials have gone into JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Barclays, and Morgan Stanley since the spring with questions about overall exposure, risk-management, and collateral quality, people familiar with the matter said.
The Fed, JPMorgan, Barclays, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.
The review was prompted in part by JPMorganâs move in March to mark down large swaths of loans in private credit portfolios, particularly those to software companies threatened by AI, the people said. The Fed has concluded its review of some of the banks, including JPM, said the people.
Itâs not uncommon for the Fed to go into banks to review their holdings, particularly when there are frequent headlines about potential risks. The Fed also does regular on-site evaluations and continually surveys for banksâ risks.
Know More
Private-credit firms are one of the fastest-growing borrower sets for banks, which were chased out of risky lending after the 2008 crisis but have since found their way back into the trade by lending to the firms that replaced them. Loans to nonbank institutions have risen from $300 billion in 2016 to more than $1.5 trillion according to FDIC data, and now account for 11% of all bank loans outstanding.
Those loans are backed by private-credit firmsâ own loans, a debt pile that has unnerved regulators. The European Central Bank also recently expanded a probe into private credit, looking at banks with exposures to the market. Last week, the Securities and Exchange Commission released a rare statement about fair value in private assets, serving as a reminder to lenders that they should be rigorous in their valuations and disclosures.
The Bank of England, during its September Financial Policy Committee meeting, said that private credit could be vulnerable to worsening financial conditions after testing the resilience of private markets.
The private credit market got slammed earlier this year when investors panicked about fundsâ exposures to software companies, which suddenly seemed obsolete amid developments in AI. The concerns caused investors in certain types of funds to pull out their money at record rates â sometimes requesting nearly 40% of a single fund in a quarter, but most funds have capped at 5%.
Private credit lenders have long been criticized for the way they value their loans, or mark them, in particular when there is disparity between where different lenders value the same loan and when a companyâs underperformance fails to translate to their marks. But lenders utilize third-party evaluators to create the marks and say they are making careful investments.
Redemption rates have declined at many of the private-credit firms and some investors have warmed to software deals again, as more of them find avenues to finance themselves both in and out of the private credit market.

07c2d66ff4db.text: By — Gerald Imray, Associated Press Gerald Imray, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/laotian-man-deported-by-u-s-to-eswatini-is-released-after-more-than-a-year-in-prison Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Laotian man deported by U.S. to Eswatini is released after more than a year in prison World Oct 5, 2026 4:01 PM EDT CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said. Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program. READ MORE: Supreme Court lets Trump continue deporting people to 3rd countries while justices consider policy Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago. Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said. Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane. "He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything," Nguyen said. "He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition." He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos. An Eswatini government spokesperson didn't immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh's release. Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said. Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations. Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far. The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent. The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back. Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn't give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December. The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held. - Published
The US says it is closely monitoring the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was concern the incident could have led to the spread of pneumonic plague, but that there was no cause for alarm.
Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said that "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".
Unconfirmed reports had suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague is found naturally among wild rodents.
No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since her death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.
The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.
Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.
Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature.
"If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."
The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.
The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago.
Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.
"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."
Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible.
"Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.

75b5ef265e81.text: States are taking on the stubbornly high fuel prices squeezing Americans ahead of the midterm elections , pushing through tax holidays and other tactics to offer relief while federal efforts have stalled. Why it matters: With November 3 less than 30 days away, the political stakes of those price-lowering levers — even if the relief is only modest — are surging amid sky-high costs. While several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at or pressed for suspending the federal gas tax, which is 18.4 cents per gallon for gas and 24.4 for diesel, Washington hasn't coalesced around a solution. Driving the news: That's left states seeking ways to give their residents relief. Case in point: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) signed a bill last week that suspends Ohio's gas tax for 90 days, an effort that earned bipartisan backing. There's an underlying election story: The state's Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, had called for a gas tax holiday, followed by her rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, announcing a plan with GOP leaders. Flashback: Georgia was the first state to suspend its fuel taxes amid the war in Iran, with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp approving a 60-day pause back in March. Since then, at least five other states (including Ohio), have suspended, lowered or stopped increases in their fuel taxes. Kemp declared a state of emergency in late September and suspended the excise tax again for 30 days. Utah cut its gas tax by some 15% through the end of the year. Gov. Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) froze an expected increase in the gas and diesel taxes in May. Illinois suspended its set increase this summer for six months. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) also suspended Indiana's gas tax in April. He renewed the suspension in late September and lifted restrictions on dyed diesel for farmers and timber harvesters. Friction point: The Trump administration signaled openness to a gas tax holiday this spring, but Congress must suspend the levy. While the idea has been floated before, lawmakers have never done so. Suspending the taxes can bring some relief to consumers, but it wouldn't offset the spikes they've felt at the pump since the start of the war. Plus, critics note doing so could increase the deficit and hurt the Highway Trust Fund it fuels. But as Axios' Ben Geman noted back in May, political winds aren't always predictable — especially with drivers and truckers still feeling the strain months later, and as political messages cluster around cost-of-living concerns. Zoom out: Other states have taken a similar approach to Braun by waiving seasonal and traditional restrictions for strained industries. For example, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) directed state law enforcement to stop enforcing rules against dyed diesel, usually reserved for off-road machinery and exempt from taxes, "to relieve the state's agricultural and timber communities." Louisiana , Nebraska , North Carolina , Oklahoma and Texas took similar action. Still, other states pursued different avenues for relief: California recently took action to permit cheaper, winter-blend gas to be sold earlier than usual, while Michigan allowed gas stations to sell lower-cost gasoline earlier this spring. The bottom line: Even if a federal gas tax holiday remains unlikely, pump pain — and perhaps, the possibility of future political pain — is fueling state action. Go deeper: Iran war drives $100 billion in extra energy costs for U.S. consumers

Tillis says his vote for Hegseth was 'biggest regret of my career' in new book Politics Oct 5, 2026 3:40 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the "biggest regret of my career" and that he also "should've stopped" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term. READ MORE: Republican North Carolina Sen. Tillis won't seek reelection after opposing Trump's bill In "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents," to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be "the lone voice in the wilderness" preventing Trump's nominees from confirmation. But he makes clear he was always skeptical about allegations about Hegseth's turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking — all of which Hegseth denied. "I know for a fact that there are others like me," Tillis writes, "Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far." He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have "expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president's actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they'd have nothing but nice things to say." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a "breaking point" with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically. Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, "my beef is not with him, but the idiots he's got working for him." He calls the president "an amazing political talent." At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to "wake up" and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, "comes back to bite the majority party in the ass." Tillis also predicts a "bloodbath" for Republicans in November's midterm elections. "All along, we've had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down," he writes. Regrets his votes for Hegseth and Kennedy The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump's tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to "intentionally sow disorder" and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets "Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way." Tillis pushed Hegseth's confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn't corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie. On his vote for Kennedy, Tillis writes that "I guess it's easy to say now, but I'm the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy's tenure has caused the country as a result." On both votes, he says he didn't want to be the deciding factor. "I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward," he writes. If you oppose Trump on everything, "you lose all influence," Tillis says. "If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape." He strongly criticizes several of Trump's other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Tillis describes his 'breaking point' over the tax bill Tillis's surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn't be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his "Big Beautiful Bill" of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn't support the bill's cuts to Medicaid. Tillis says he thought to himself, "I'm done." "Everyone reaches a breaking point," he writes. He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied "I am! DJT." In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a "QUITTER!" on social media, among other insults. Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat.
On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them.
That parliamentary result confirmed that SÃ¡nchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority.
But as has so often been the case throughout SÃ¡nchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre.
His government has been struggling in recent months.
His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos CerdÃ¡n and JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, JosÃ© Luis RodrÃguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing.
In addition, SÃ¡nchez's wife, BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that GÃ³mez and SÃ¡nchez vehemently deny.
Meanwhile, SÃ¡nchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister.
Although SÃ¡nchez had insisted until recently that he would see out the legislature and not call elections until next summer, his government had looked increasingly unlikely to make it that far.
The wave of outrage which has exploded in recent days over housing has provided him with the ideal reason to call elections early - and a welcome issue away from Ceuta and the allegations of corruption.
Appealing to his own party's voters and those further to the left on Monday, he called for voters to "mobilise and ensure that parliament gives us a much bigger, progressive majority with which to defeat the elites, conquer social rights and keep transforming Spain".
On the upcoming campaign trail, SÃ¡nchez can point to the fact that his adversaries on the right - such as the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox - voted against his government's housing measures, which sought to prevent the eviction of tenants, improving the conditions of their contracts and preventing investors from buying residential property.
The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the SÃ¡nchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists.
However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that SÃ¡nchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive.
Earlier this year, when SÃ¡nchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then.
However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left.
Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides SÃ¡nchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career.

Reflection AI, the startup billing itself as Americaâs answer to open-source Chinese AI, is releasing its first model, called Beam.
The company, founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers, is positioning Beam as a âworkhorseâ that performs better than other Western open models. The model is particularly strong at coding and agentic tasks, cofounder and CEO Misha Laskin told Semafor. It also needs three to four times less computing power to reason through a problem than comparable open models, he said, making it faster and cheaper to run.
The modelâs capabilities are comparable to one of Chinaâs Z.aiâs recent models, GLM-5.2, which was released in June; Beam is âapproachingâ the performance of Alibabaâs most advanced model, Qwen 3.8-Max, which trails the top closed American models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
Chinaâs startups and tech giants have led the world in open-source AI. Several large Western companies have recently embraced Chinese models as a way to reduce costs for certain repetitive tasks like customer service and writing routine code. Beijing has also promoted open source as a diplomatic tool to help other countries in their tech development. But because open models can be downloaded and run with fewer safeguards, their rise has also raised security concerns: US and UK government evaluators found that recent Chinese models could help hackers exploit code vulnerabilities.
New York-based Reflection sees a large market in businesses, governments, and other entities building sovereign AI systems that donât or canât use Chinese models, but still want to âownâ and control how they use AI, Laskin said.
âThey donât really have very good options today,â he said.
Reflection is already training its next model, which Laskin said would be âmuch moreâ powerful and performant than Beam.
Know More
The startup, which has investments from Nvidia, Sequoia, and Citigroup, in June confirmed it closed its latest funding round at a $25 billion pre-money valuation. With Beamâs release, Reflection joins a slate of other Western startups, including Thinking Machines Lab and Mistral, that also offer open-weight AI models.
Its release comes as calls for AI regulation reach a fever pitch in the US, after a slate of alarming security incidents. The leading US AI labs and tech companies signed what US President Donald Trump called a âmorally bindingâ agreement on safety principles following a White House meeting.
Trump has pushed for companies to regulate themselves, rather than subject them to federal oversight, but the political calculus could shift quickly should the Democrats take over Congress in November.
Reflection says it wants to enable âbuilders of open models to be able to contribute to the discourse that is happening in DC on regulation,â Laskin said.
âYou want multiple voices around the table, both open and closed, and they should be working collaboratively on helping the government regulate AI,â he said. âWe see this entrance as something that enables more open model perspectives to be part of the discourse in DC.â
Laskin said Reflection is working with both the US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence and the UKâs AI Safety Institute to assess the modelâs capabilities.

It's an issue that is top of mind for voters worried that their groundwater here is being polluted by the industry's waste. Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor, is tapping into the angst as part of her appeal to conservative areas that she hopes will be part of a victory in the Republican-leaning state. "We will all pay for this mistake. So that's why we must act now." She got some help during the recent appearance, Acton's fourth to the Appalachian county that hasn't backed Democrats in years. She was joined by Susan Vessels, a prominent local Republican who had decided to forgo her own party's nominee for governor, tech billionaire and former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. Vessels, president of the city council in Marietta, praised Acton for her willingness to listen to local residents' concerns about the risks posed by fracking. She said she and others have been frustrated in their attempts to get lawmakers to do the same. "It is a pro-drinking water position, and it should be easy for any leader to support," Vessels said. Ramaswamy has been a strong supporter of developing American energy sources, including through fracking: "Unlock American energy. More recently in Marietta, he said he wants an economic boom that protects Ohio's natural resources and "the water quality of our communities." Ramaswamy, who has been endorsed by Trump, hosted a veterans' town hall there on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terror attacks. "Voters are frustrated, and it's not just with one political party," Ramaswamy campaign manager Jonathan Ewing said. "They're frustrated by an insider system that they see as working for one connected class of people and not for them." He said Ramaswamy is from outside that system and "can't be bought." Ramaswamy, who has landed endorsements from farming groups and the National Rifle Association, also made a stop at Schafer Leather, a thriving downtown business where customers can buy cowboy boots, wallets, belts or a Gun Tote'n Mama handbag. Staff members say they're fully in the GOP nominee's corner, despite concerns over the soaring price of gas since Trump launched the Iran war. Sherry Bailey, the store's 62-year-old sales clerk, said her core values align best with the GOP. "I believe in the Lord and the family and being free Americans," she said. Democrats target voters who believe they're being ignored That sort of party loyalty has only seemed to grow in Ohio during the Trump era, as he has won increasing shares of the vote in counties such as Washington, where he got 71% support in 2024. They say rural areas where residents are now represented by Republican majorities from their county commissions to the statehouse to Congress are growing weary of one-party rule. They identified disaffected Democrats, engaged but undecided independents and legacy Republicans, who he defined as those "disgusted with how they've seen their party go into the MAGAsphere." Pentagon, FBI personnel-data breaches raise questions
The defense breach, which exposed about 3 million people, went undetected for months.
A Pentagon breach that exposed sensitive personnel information for months is raising questions yet again about federal agencies' ability to detect unauthorized access to their records.
Information about roughly 3 million people was potentially exposed from October 2025 to July 16, 2026, by a breach of a file-sharing system at the Defense Manpower Data Center, which maintains personnel information used across the military and other government agencies.
“Three million people may be the headline, but months of unauthorized access to highly sensitive data going undetected is the real warning,” said Nitay Milner, co-founder and CEO of data security company ORION Security.
Nextgov/FCW obtained a copy of the letter, which was signed by DMDC Director Katie Griffin. The accessed files contained unencrypted personal information, including Social Security numbers and, depending on the individual, names, birth dates, contact information and military occupational specialties.
“Upon discovery of the security vulnerability, DMDC immediately initiated privacy and cybersecurity incident response actions in accordance with Office of the Management and Budget and [Defense] Department guidelines and policies,” Griffin wrote. “We are taking appropriate actions to assess and enhance the cybersecurity posture of the DMDC system.”
DMDC patched the flaw and restored the system, according to the letter, and affected individuals are being offered a year of credit monitoring and identity-restoration services.
Military Times first reported the incident late last month, citing the same notice. A defense official later told CNN that the breach affected 2.76 million living people and another 294,000 deceased individuals.
The disclosure comes as the FBI responds to a separate breach claimed by prolific cybercrime group ShinyHunters, which likely exposed sensitive records of personnel involved in intelligence-gathering roles.
No public evidence has linked the intrusions, though both cases involve information that could help attackers identify government personnel and tailor attempts to deceive them through fraud schemes. Such data can also identify employees whose work is of particular interest to foreign intelligence services.
The breach is hardly the first to expose weaknesses in federal systems in recent years. In December 2024, Treasury disclosed that Chinese state-sponsored hackers accessed unclassified documents through a compromised remote-support service. Separately, the federal judiciary acknowledged attacks on its electronic case management system in August 2025, and the Congressional Budget Office confirmed unauthorized access to its systems that November.
AI systems are widely expected to accelerate cyberattacks, helping hackers find security weaknesses and use stolen personal information to make their targeting more precise and convincing.
Milner said detecting unauthorized activity requires agencies to understand who is gathering sensitive information, whether they are permitted to enter a given system and whether their behavior makes sense.
That scrutiny can matter even when an intrusion doesn’t immediately disrupt a system or draw attention. In the case of DMDC, the department’s notification described access spanning roughly nine months before the vulnerability was discovered.
Jeff Wichman, senior director of breach preparedness and response at Semperis, said agencies must plan for intrusions even when they have experienced security teams and established protections.
“The FBI and Pentagon have amazing responders, but these breaches are still happening and eventually everyone is hit,” he said. “True resilience depends on having a fully pressure-tested incident response plan detailing exactly which teams are responsible for what across the entire breach cycle, from initial discovery and containment to legal and regulatory reporting.”
He also warned that new government AI services, including the America.gov chatbot, could create more ways for attackers to reach sensitive information if those tools connect to agency systems. “More government agencies will fall victim to compromise,” he said. “Every piece of leaked data creates a domino effect.”

READ MORE: A Russian report says a worker at a Siberian plague research institute fell ill and died of an unknown cause On Oct. 2, Igor Kobzev, governor of the Irkutsk Oblast region, confirmed via a Telegram post that he was hosting an "extraordinary meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission" with the head of Rospotrebnadzor. The country's chief sanitary doctor, Anna Yuryevna Popova, was in attendance. Kobzev said the meeting occurred after information emerged "about a suspected case of a regional resident with a particularly dangerous infection." He described the situation as "under strict control," and said the consumer protection agency had implemented "a full range of anti-epidemic measures." That same day, Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the neighboring Republic of Buryatia, described the woman's death as being caused by the "plague," as he was responding to reports that she had previously traveled to the region. News outlets say Tsydenov later edited the post adding the word "possibly." "There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in the area bordering Mongolia," he said. "The source of the infection is circumstances unrelated to Buryatia." On Oct. 4, Rospotrebnadzor told state news agency TASS that it was responding to a case involving a lab employee "who was diagnosed with pneumonia of unknown etiology." The agency did not mention the woman's death. On Monday, Kobzev echoed the consumer protection agency's wording, but described it as the woman's cause of death. He clarified that "microorganisms associated with her professional activities were not detected in the patient's samples," and that no employees from the institute had sought medical attention in the past several days. Local officials warned people not to visit the town of Shelekhov in a Telegram post that they later deleted, according to independent local news outlet People of Baikal. What have local and independent media outlets said? People of Baikal identified the worker as a 28-year-old lab technician and said she died of the pneumonic plague. The news outlet cited local journalist Pavel Stepanov, who reported the lab worker was infected after she broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague bacterium. It also reported that a state television channel deleted five articles it had published about the incident. Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement to TASS that the institute had identified "no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms." Health authorities hospitalized 189 people who had been in contact with the lab worker, according to The Moscow Times, an independent Russian news outlet. Local news outlet IrCity reported that a city cleanup event had been canceled as part of safety measures being taken "due to the unfavorable epidemiological situation." What is the pneumonic plague? Plague is a severe and often fatal disease caused by a bacteria known as Yersinia pestis, which is often found in small mammals and fleas, according to the World Health Organization. People are infected through bites from infected fleas, contact with infected tissues or inhalation of infected respiratory particles. There are three main kinds of plague: bubonic, pneumonic and septicaemic. Bubonic plague is the likely cause of the Black Death, the pandemic that hit Europe in the mid-1300s. READ MORE: The U.S. sees 7 plague cases a year. Here's why Pneumonic plague is a respiratory disease characterized by rapidly developing pneumonia, shortness of breath, chest pain and cough, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

95e5c195d4ec.text: An intra-party debate over how best to deflect Republican attacks on transgender issues has Democrats angrily sniping at each other just weeks out from the midterm elections. Why it matters: This is not the position Democrats hoped to be in two years after their 2024 election loss , which many in the party attributed to being outflanked by GOP messaging on trans issues. "People feel you need to respond in some way to some of these attacks because people didn't do it two years ago," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a co-chair of the Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, told Axios. "But you also need to realize what we're winning on right now," Pocan added, saying Democratic candidates need to strike "a balance." "Silence is deadly, and I think we played that out in 2024," said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at the centrist think tank Third Way, citing polling that found most voters believed Democrats "thought there should be no rules in sports, no rules around health care." Driving the news: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) set off a firestorm in her district and on Capitol Hill in September by stating in a direct-to-camera ad that she "voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools." "Parents know what's best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls' sports," Kaptur said in the spot — a response to an ad from Republican Derek Merrin that said she "voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports." Multiple county parties condemned the ad — particularly the reference to transgender girls as "boys" — and urged Kaptur to take it down. One LGBTQ+ group, the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, said in a statement there is "no difference" between Kaptur and Merrin because they are "both united against the LBTQIA+ community." What they're saying: "The ads were deeply offensive to the Equality Caucus and the broader LGBTQ community that we represent," said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the caucus' political arm, Equality PAC. He told Axios: "The Equality Caucus is not going to stand by passively and allow anyone to scapegoat the trans community. It is a red line for us." Equality PAC "is absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time," the group said in a separate statement to Axios, calling Kaptur's language "unacceptable." What we're hearing: Kaptur's colleagues also privately communicated their disgust with the ad to her office, multiple House Democrats familiar with the matter told Axios. The lawmakers predicted there will be in-person conversations with Kaptur when the House returns in November, especially if she wins her election. "Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls' sports stay fair," said Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer. "She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor." Zoom out: It's not just Kaptur. Democratic House candidates Blake Gendebien of New York and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, and Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, have put out ads featuring similar rhetoric. Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) released an ad last week in which he said there are "real concerns about fairness and safety" and that "states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls." That ad, like Kaptur's, raised eyebrows privately among LGBTQ+ House Democrats, though none have called him out publicly for it. The other side: Centrist groups and lawmakers say the party has to be realistic about districts like Kaptur's, which President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024. "Marcy Kaptur and Don Davis are doing the most important work in Democratic politics: winning Trump districts," said Liam Kerr, cofounder of centrist group Welcome PAC. Kerr argued attacks from LGBTQ+ groups will only help swing-district Democrats: "Taking the 20% side of an 80/20 issue may be bad politics, but elevating the big winners repudiating you is even worse advocacy." Between the lines: "Our latest [research] showed that anti-trans attacks take about 8 points off of the Democratic vote if you just let it sit out there," Erickson, the Third Way official, told Axios. "But there are ways to respond that get you back up 10 to 12 to 14 points," she continued. "There are a bunch of different ways to say it ... just being clear that there need to be rules. Not laws, but rules." "When it comes to health care, that parents, not politicians, should be in charge of decisions about their kids' health care." The bottom line: Centrists and LGBTQ+ Democrats alike say a careful balance can and should be struck. Several lawmakers pointed to Senate hopefuls James Talarico and Sherrod Brown as examples for deftly maneuvering on this issue. Erickson said "calling transgender girls 'boys' ... is not respectful" and that candidates "don't have to do it. There's better ways to talk about this."

49e67e30ebc2.text: By — Joseph Wilson, Associated Press Joseph Wilson, Associated Press By — Alicia León, Associated Press Alicia León, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-to-know-about-spains-housing-protests-sparked-by-an-87-year-old-womans-eviction Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about Spain's housing protests sparked by an 87-year-old woman's eviction World Oct 5, 2026 8:12 PM EDT MADRID, Spain (AP) — Tens of thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of various cities in Spain to demand help for renters, after lawmakers rejected a package of emergency measures aimed at tackling the nation's housing affordability crisis. READ MORE: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks encampment protest in Madrid over housing crisis Large crowds marched in Madrid calling for a general strike and affordable housing. In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse protesters who broke through the security perimeter outside the City of Arts and Sciences, a futuristic complex by famed architect Santiago Calatrava, where a real estate summit was being held. Images showed altercations between police and protesters, with officers using batons to strike demonstrators, who threw barriers. There were no immediate reports of injuries. Public outrage over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman has put Spain's progressive government under immense pressure to tackle the nation's entrenched housing cost crisis. On Monday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced early elections to take place on Nov. 29, aiming to seize on his base's anger over the rejected housing measures. Around 1,000 protesters have spent the past week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol, one of the capital's most popular public spaces, after María del Carmen Abascal was evicted from her home of seven decades in downtown Madrid on Sept. 23. The protesters say they won't leave until the government takes real steps to protect tenants. A similar encampment has cropped up in Barcelona's Plaza Catalunya. The Sánchez-led government responded with emergency measures aimed at restricting evictions, curbing property speculation and giving renters indefinite leases, among other measures. But conservative opposition parties joined forces to reject the ratification of the measures in parliament on Friday. Here is what to know about Spain's housing crisis and the political battle over how to address it. Spain is hard-hit due to small rental market The housing crunch has been simmering for years in Spain, eating into household budgets and angering voters. While many countries have similar circumstances, Spain's poorest and its young are being particularly impacted, because they can't afford to purchase a home and are being squeezed by the country's small stock of rental properties. The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years. The price per square meter has risen from 8.20 euros (now $9.30) in 2016 to 15.10 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista. Spain's government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so. Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development for government-owned rental properties, which represent less than 2% of its available stock. The EU average is 8%. Maricarmen set the spark Tens of thousands of people periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers and blaming real estate speculators as well as tourist apartment platforms like Airbnb for rising rents. But a new wave of indignation swept Spain when Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her apartment after police cordoned off the street. Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country. "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," Abascal said in a video recorded from a hospital bed after the eviction. The Spanish real estate company which had insisted on evicting her in order to rent the property at a much higher price ended up reaching an agreement for her to return to the apartment, her lawyer said, adding that Abascal was "happy." She has yet to be discharged from the hospital. Even with a satisfying resolution for "Maricarmen," as Abascal is now widely known, she remains the embodiment of the struggle against suffocating rental costs. Protesters have carried signs with slogans such as "Not even one more Maricarmen!" and demonstrations have been cropping up in cities across the country. Joseph Wilson reported from Barcelona. Renata Brito contributed to this report from Barcelona. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. a8cfab7f6c3f.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/no-arrests-after-georgia-block-party-shooting-as-police-pursue-who-killed-2-and-injured-dozens Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter No arrests after Georgia block party shooting as police pursue who killed 2 and injured dozens Nation Oct 5, 2026 7:43 PM EDT VIENNA, Ga. (AP) — Whoever opened fire at a sprawling block party in rural southern Georgia over the weekend, killing two people and leaving nearly three dozen others injured, remained at large Monday as authorities offered no new information about the shootings. No arrests have been announced in Dooly County, where the sheriff says more than 50 shots were fired early Sunday in the small city of Vienna as more than 1,000 celebrated a homecoming football victory long after midnight. READ MORE: Teen gets life without parole for killing 4 in shooting at Georgia's Apalachee High School Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy identified the two people killed as Ja'Quavion Jackson, 21, of Cordele, and Macaleb Jackson, 23, of Hawkinsville. The two men don't appear to be related, said Sara Lue, a spokesperson for the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. An additional 35 people were injured — most of them by gunfire, though others were hurt in the chaotic scramble to flee, authorities told reporters at a Sunday news conference. The sheriff said an unspecified number were hospitalized with critical injuries. Authorities haven't said what may have motivated the shootings or whether they're looking for a lone gunman or multiple shooters. They also have not said precisely how many people were shot. "At large parties with people from different places, not just your locals, sometimes problems come," Peavy said Sunday. Local officials say the block party wasn't a school-sponsored event and didn't have a city permit. Peavy said he had extra deputies working over the weekend in anticipation of homecoming drawing large numbers of alumni and other out-of-town visitors. The sheriff did not immediately return a phone message Monday. Lue said no further updates were available from state investigators, who customarily assist Georgia's rural communities in major cases. The violence marred what Peavy said had been a large but otherwise peaceful celebration of Dooly County High School winning its homecoming football game in Vienna, a city of about 3,000 people located about 50 miles (80 kilometers) south of Macon. Crowds of revelers gathered across an area covering four blocks, and Peavy said that he had deputies patrolling the area. When the first shots were fired and deputies rushed to the scene, he said, more gunfire sounded about a block away. "It was so many people," Peavy said. "And it was just hard to figure out what was going on." Among this weekend's visitors was Antoria Felton of Jonesboro, who drove two hours to bring her daughter and six other girls to Vienna. She told WMAZ-TV that everything seemed peaceful when suddenly "bullets were going everywhere." Felton said she saw that "kids laying on the ground had been shot" as she scrambled to find her daughter and the other girls. "The only thing I'm trying to do is find these girls," Felton said. "Everybody scattered out everywhere, everybody running. It was terrifying." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. be37f5bdd86f.text: By — Hannah Grabenstein Hannah Grabenstein Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/helpful-or-harmful-when-it-comes-to-ai-and-young-kids-experts-have-these-tips-for-parents Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Helpful or harmful? When it comes to AI and young kids, experts have these tips for parents Education Oct 5, 2026 10:03 PM EDT While much advice and research around artificial intelligence and kids tend to focus on older kids and teens, a lot of critical brain development happens before age 8 — making those early years a key window to help kids understand what AI is and isn't, experts say. Young children are encountering AI in their day-to-day lives at home, in child care or at school. That includes smart assistants like Amazon's Alexa or Apple's Siri, or generative AI content they may find while watching YouTube. READ MORE: Don't know how to talk to your tween about AI? Here's where to start, according to experts By the time that a child is preschool age, they have the ability to learn information from technology, said Lauren Girouard, a researcher at Harvard Graduate School of Education and the University of Michigan who studies how children 12 and under interact with digital information. And though overall research on young children and AI is still developing, particularly in psychology, there's growing early evidence that children process information from AI material in the same way they do other technology, Girouard added. "We know that AI-powered learning tutors can be really valuable," Girouard said. "But what we know about kids' interactions with the very personal, at-home AI that we've had since the advent of ChatGPT at the end of 2022 is an entirely different ballgame that we're still learning about." Experts who spoke to PBS News offered some tips on how to have age-appropriate conversations about this technology with young children. Teach around the AI they already encounter If you have a smart speaker with an AI assistant, like Alexa or Siri, use your interactions with it as a way to distinguish between human and computer responses, said Jennifer Katzenstein, co-director of the Center for Behavioral Health at Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital. In these moments, "it's worth explaining: That's the computer answering," she said. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Katzenstein also suggested encouraging the child to ask another adult what they think too, which teaches kids to "understand there's a human response, and then there's a computer response." Especially with children younger than 5, parents can also help kids understand that AI is able to tell stories or answer questions, but just because it has a friendly voice, that doesn't mean it's a human. Young children might already be talking to relatives on the phone or over video, so it's important to explain the difference between a device that allows human-to-human communication versus a machine, said Dr. Jenny Radesky, division director of developmental behavioral pediatrics at the University of Michigan School of Medicine. Until her son was 7, she said, he thought Siri was "an actual woman who lived in California." "Little kids are much more magical thinkers," Radesky said. And because they attribute more human-like qualities onto technologies, they can start to develop parasocial attachments to devices that sound like humans, she added. WATCH: Teachers and parents weigh benefits and risks of artificial intelligence in schools Use concrete terms that kids will understand to explain that AI isn't human, Radesky said. You can remind them that even though it sounds like you're talking with a human, the machine has never been sad, doesn't know what it's like to snuggle and doesn't have a body or soul. Radesky suggested choosing a different "wake word" for your smart speaker, if possible, to something other than a human name. (Her colleague renamed his device "Computer," to shift away from using a prompt like "Hey, Siri.") Another option: Forgo the smart devices entirely, said Dr. Molly O'Shea, a pediatrician who works with the American Academy of Pediatrics on children and AI use. "I actually encourage parents — when a child comes to them and asks a question that the parent doesn't know the answer to — to actually go through the process of guessing the answer, thinking through, problem solving out loud," O'Shea said. Stay away from AI toys, at least for now There's not enough research to suggest that AI toys are broadly beneficial to children right now, experts say. Common Sense Media, which conducts risk assessments for AI products, released guidance earlier this year that urges parents to keep AI toys away from children aged 5 and younger, and to "exercise extreme caution" when purchasing them for 6 to 12 year-olds. They tested "three AI companion toys," some of which were "cuddly, colorful and feature[d] kids 3 to 8 in their advertising." But young children "lack the cognitive development" to use the torys safely, the report noted. In general, AI toys pose an "unacceptable risk" to children, getting past guardrails around sensitive topics, the group said. Its testing found that 27% of the toy responses were inappropriate for children, and were "too mature, complex, or scary" for young kids. AI toys can also pose privacy risks by collecting data on children and may set unrealistic expectations by creating dependency and making "real relationships seem difficult" in comparison to technology that doesn't say no and is always available. READ MORE: 'It's deeply disturbing.' What a new report says about risks Google's AI search features pose to kids Preparing children how to think about AI toys is useful, Katzenstein said, since they may encounter them at a friend's house or
